text: On the defendant's motion, a district court may vacate any judgment and grant a new trial when the interest of justice requires it.
known_limitations: The rule does not itself define every merits standard encompassed by the interest of justice.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of Rule 33(a).

text: After a nonjury trial, the court may take additional testimony and enter a new judgment.
known_limitations: Applies only when the case was tried without a jury.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of Rule 33(a).

text: A motion grounded on newly discovered evidence must be filed within three years after the verdict or finding of guilty.
known_limitations: Ground characterization and merits standards require controlling-circuit authority.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of Rule 33(b)(1).

text: If an appeal is pending, the district court may not grant a newly-discovered-evidence motion until the appellate court remands the case.
known_limitations: The rule bars granting; it does not state that filing or denial is barred. Rule 37 and Appellate Rule 12.1 interaction remains to be verified.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of the second sentence of Rule 33(b)(1).

text: A Rule 33 motion based on any ground other than newly discovered evidence must be filed within fourteen days after the verdict or finding of guilty.
known_limitations: Subject to current Rule 45 computation and extension provisions.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of Rule 33(b)(2).

text: Both Rule 33 filing periods run from the verdict or finding of guilty, not from sentencing, entry of judgment, or completion of an appeal.
known_limitations: The date must be established from the actual docket; this claim does not resolve later amended or partial verdicts.
researcher_notes: Negative clarification based on the express trigger in both parts of Rule 33(b).

text: For a Rule 33 period stated in days, Rule 45 excludes the triggering day, counts every intervening day, and carries the deadline to the next non-weekend, non-holiday day when the last day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday.
known_limitations: Clerk-office inaccessibility and local last-day filing mechanics require separate Rule 45 and local-rule review.
researcher_notes: Paraphrase of Rule 45(a)(1).

text: Rule 45(b)(1) lets the court extend a time on its own, or for good cause on a party's motion made before the time expires or, after it expires, if the party failed to act because of excusable neglect; Rule 45(b)(2)'s exception, which bars extending the time to take any action under Rule 35 except as stated in that rule, applies to Rule 35, not Rule 33. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 45(b) (Dec. 1, 2025 ed.)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Whether good cause or excusable neglect exists is fact-specific and circuit law may supply the application factors.
researcher_notes: Current Rule 45 text corrects the legacy statement that a late Rule 33 motion is categorically barred. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30. Revised 2026-11-02 under the Nov. 1, 2026 double legal review, as checked against the saved sources; owner approved 2026-11-02; double legal review completed; licensed-attorney approval not recorded.

text: Rule 33's filing deadline is a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule: a properly raised timeliness objection must be enforced, but the objection can be forfeited.
known_limitations: Eberhart's numerical deadlines and Rule 45 language are superseded; only the jurisdiction and forfeiture holding is used.
researcher_notes: Holding at 546 U.S. 13, 15-19.

text: Rule 33(a) authorizes a new trial only "[u]pon the defendant's motion," and the 1966 Advisory Committee Note states that a judge has no power to order a new trial on his own motion, while leaving intact the court's power in certain circumstances, before verdict or finding of guilty, to declare a mistrial and order a new trial on its own motion. Construing the earlier rule, *Smith* held that the Government was entitled to writs vacating a new-trial order the district judge entered on his own initiative after the conviction had been affirmed and the defendant had been imprisoned, reasoning that "expiration of the time within which relief can openly be asked of the judge, terminates the time within which it can properly be granted on the court's own initiative." [Fed. R. Crim. P. 33(a) & advisory committee's note to 1966 amendment](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title18/pdf/USCODE-2024-title18-app.pdf); [*United States v. Smith*, 331 U.S. 469, 470–71, 475, 477 (1947)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-331/pdf/USREPORTS-331-469.pdf)
known_limitations: Smith construed the 1946 rule; the current rule now expressly predicates relief on the defendant's motion.
researcher_notes: Holding and current-text cross-check. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: A Rule 33 new trial is sought by the defendant's motion under the Criminal Rules, which govern the procedure in all criminal proceedings in the United States district courts; on that motion, "the court may vacate any judgment and grant a new trial if the interest of justice so requires." [Fed. R. Crim. P. 1(a)(1), 33(a) (Dec. 1, 2025 ed.)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: This claim does not resolve reassignment, recusal, transfer, or appellate-remand mechanics.
researcher_notes: Institutional scope from Rule 1(a)(1) read with Rule 33's post-trial motion text. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30. Revised 2026-11-02 under the Nov. 1, 2026 double legal review, as checked against the saved sources; owner approved 2026-11-02; double legal review completed; licensed-attorney approval not recorded.

text: Sections 2244(b)(1) and (b)(2) apply by their terms to second or successive habeas applications under § 2254, and § 2244(d) applies to applications by persons in custody pursuant to state-court judgments.
known_limitations: This claim identifies express statutory subjects; it does not resolve every cross-reference or case-law application.
researcher_notes: Direct text of § 2244(b)(1), (b)(2), and (d).

text: Before a second or successive § 2254 application is filed in district court, the applicant must move in the appropriate court of appeals for an order authorizing the district court to consider it.
known_limitations: This direct § 2244(b)(3)(A) claim is framed for the § 2254 application expressly governed by subsection (b).
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 2244(b)(3)(A).

text: The court of appeals must assign the authorization motion to a three-judge panel.
known_limitations: Panel composition and internal assignment procedures are not addressed.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 2244(b)(3)(B).

text: The panel may authorize filing only if it determines that the applicant has made a prima facie showing that the application satisfies § 2244(b)'s requirements.
known_limitations: Circuit-specific definitions and application of prima facie remain unverified.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 2244(b)(3)(C).

text: Section 2244(b)(3)(D) directs the court of appeals to grant or deny authorization not later than thirty days after the motion is filed.
known_limitations: No jurisdictional classification, enforceability conclusion, or remedy for noncompliance is stated; circuit-specific authority is required.
researcher_notes: Records the statutory command only.

text: For the state-prisoner authorization decision governed directly by § 2244(b)(3), subsection (E) says the grant or denial is not appealable and may not be the subject of rehearing or certiorari.
known_limitations: Bowe requires a distinct analysis for federal § 2255(h) authorization decisions.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 2244(b)(3)(E), limited to the statute's state track.

text: After the court of appeals authorizes a state-prisoner claim, the district court must dismiss that authorized claim unless the applicant shows that it satisfies § 2244(b)'s requirements.
known_limitations: This claim does not decide treatment of claims outside the appellate authorization or the federal § 2255 procedure.
researcher_notes: Corrects the legacy inversion of § 2244(b)(4)'s authorized-claim text.

text: A second or successive § 2255 motion must be certified as provided in § 2244 by a panel of the appropriate court of appeals to contain either qualifying newly discovered evidence under § 2255(h)(1) or a qualifying new rule of constitutional law under § 2255(h)(2).
known_limitations: This claim does not determine whether a filing is second or successive or whether either gate is met.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 2255(h).

text: Section 2244(b)(3)(E) does not bar Supreme Court certiorari review of a federal prisoner's request to file a successive § 2255 motion.
known_limitations: This holding does not imply that certiorari will be granted or that other review routes are available.
researcher_notes: Bowe first holding, official preliminary print at 607 U.S. 19-32.

text: Section 2244(b)(1)'s previously-presented-claim bar does not apply to successive motions filed by federal prisoners under § 2255(h).
known_limitations: Every claim still must satisfy § 2255(h); Bowe did not eliminate other procedural or merits requirements.
researcher_notes: Bowe second holding, official preliminary print at 607 U.S. 32-38.

text: The Supreme Court vacated and remanded for the Eleventh Circuit to decide Bowe's authorization request under the correct standard; the Supreme Court did not itself authorize his successive motion.
known_limitations: The Eleventh Circuit's post-remand disposition is outside this claim and must be checked separately before use.
researcher_notes: Disposition at 607 U.S. 38.

text: Bowe distinguished § 2244(b)(3)(E)'s rehearing language from its certiorari language and did not decide whether that rehearing bar applies to federal-prisoner authorization decisions.
known_limitations: A circuit-specific answer requires that circuit's current rules and precedent.
researcher_notes: Holding boundary from 607 U.S. 29-30; this prevents overreading Bowe.

text: Section 2244(d)'s one-year limitation and statutory tolling provisions govern the state-judgment track described there; they are not the limitation provisions for a federal prisoner's § 2255 motion.
known_limitations: This claim does not state or analyze § 2255(f)'s separate limitations rules.
researcher_notes: Direct scope of § 2244(d).

text: The state-prisoner substantive gates in § 2244(b)(2) and the federal-prisoner gates in § 2255(h) are not identically worded, so a federal § 2255(h) analysis must use § 2255(h)'s substantive requirements rather than silently substituting § 2244(b)(2).
known_limitations: Case-law interpretation of each gate remains to be researched.
researcher_notes: Side-by-side statutory-text comparison.

text: Section 3624(a) directs the Bureau of Prisons to release a prisoner when the term of imprisonment expires, less credit toward service of the sentence provided by § 3624(b).
known_limitations: Weekend and holiday release mechanics are not included.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 3624(a).

text: A prisoner serving more than one year, other than a life term, may receive up to fifty-four days of GCT for each year of the sentence imposed by the court, subject to the Bureau's determination of exemplary compliance with institutional disciplinary regulations.
known_limitations: Offense-date and literacy rules must also be applied.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 3624(b)(1).

text: If the Bureau determines that the prisoner did not satisfactorily comply during the relevant year, the prisoner receives no GCT or a lesser amount the Bureau determines appropriate; the Bureau also must consider high-school-diploma progress, and credit not earned may not later be granted.
known_limitations: Actual disciplinary and literacy determinations require the record and regulations.
researcher_notes: Direct statutory conditions.

text: Subject to § 3624(b)(2), the statute directs that credit for the last year of a term be credited on the first day of the last year.
known_limitations: Current regulation separately controls partial-final-year proration and anniversary mechanics.
researcher_notes: Statutory timing text, not a no-proration claim.

text: GCT awarded under § 3624(b) after enactment of the Prison Litigation Reform Act vests on the date the prisoner is released from custody.
known_limitations: Earlier offense-date branches may have distinct annual vesting rules under the regulation.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 3624(b)(2).

text: For offenses committed on or after November 1, 1987, 28 C.F.R. § 523.20(b)(1) directs the Bureau to project the maximum possible GCT from the imposed sentence while recognizing that the projected release date can change during incarceration.
known_limitations: This does not calculate an individual release date.
researcher_notes: Current 2025 CFR text cross-checked to 2022 final rule.

text: The Bureau awards prorated GCT for a partial final year of the sentence imposed.
known_limitations: Exact proration and rounding require the Bureau computation.
researcher_notes: Corrects the legacy no-proration implication.

text: Under the regulation, an inmate may receive up to fifty-four days on each anniversary date; last-year credit is awarded after the final anniversary period unless the final year is complete, in which case it is awarded on the first day of that final anniversary period.
known_limitations: All awards remain subject to conduct and literacy conditions.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 523.20(b)(3).

text: For an offense committed on or after April 26, 1996, the regulation sets a maximum of fifty-four days per imposed-sentence year when the literacy condition is met and forty-two days when it is not, subject to the regulation's final-removal-order exception.
known_limitations: The 1994-1996 branch and Part 544 literacy definitions require separate application.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 523.20(d)(2)-(3).

text: The First Step Act changed GCT from a time-served calculation to a sentence-imposed calculation, made the amendment applicable to offenses committed before, on, or after enactment except offenses before November 1, 1987, and the change took effect when the risk-and-needs system was released on July 19, 2019.
known_limitations: D.C. Code and pre-November 1987 rules are outside this claim.
researcher_notes: Public Law supplies amendment, effectiveness condition, and applicability; BOP official source supplies release date of the assessment system.

text: Barber v. Thomas upheld the Bureau's time-served method under the pre-First Step Act text, but the First Step Act superseded that calculation rule for covered current sentences.
known_limitations: Barber remains relevant to the former statutory text, not the current covered calculation.
researcher_notes: Historical holding and statutory supersession separated.

text: The regulation permits GCT reduction for qualifying disciplinary sanctions or failure to comply with applicable literacy requirements.
known_limitations: Part 541 procedure, sanction validity, and restoration are outside this claim.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 523.20(a).

text: Good-conduct-time credit under § 3624(b) is distinct from First Step Act time credits, which are earned through evidence-based recidivism reduction programming or productive activities under § 3632(d)(4) and applied toward prerelease custody or supervised release under § 3624(g). [18 U.S.C. § 3624(b), (g)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3624); [18 U.S.C. § 3632(d)(4), (d)(6)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3632); [28 C.F.R. § 523.20](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title28-vol2/pdf/CFR-2025-title28-vol2-sec523-30.pdf)
known_limitations: The separate time-credit eligibility and application rules are outside this module.
researcher_notes: Explicit distinction in the 2022 final rule preamble. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Section 3632(a) required the Attorney General, in consultation with the Independent Review Committee, to develop and publicly release the risk-and-needs assessment system no later than 210 days after enactment.
known_limitations: This claim states the statutory development deadline, not an individualized implementation remedy.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 3632(a).

text: The system must reassess each prisoner's recidivism risk periodically using indicators of progress and regression that are dynamic and reasonably expected to change in prison.
known_limitations: A particular assessment or scoring method is not validated.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 3632(a)(4).

text: The Department of Justice published the First Step Act Risk and Needs Assessment System on July 19, 2019; the new tool the Bureau of Prisons would use under that system is called PATTERN, and DOJ described the publication as a key requirement of the First Step Act. [U.S. Department of Justice PATTERN publication record (July 19, 2019)](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/department-justice-announces-release-3100-inmates-under-first-step-act-publishes-risk-and)
known_limitations: Later implementation and individual assessments are distinct questions.
researcher_notes: Corrects the legacy conflation of PATTERN publication with the 2022 FTC regulation. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Except for a prisoner made ineligible by § 3632(d)(4)(D), successful participation earns ten days of FTCs for every thirty days of qualifying evidence-based recidivism-reduction programming or productive activities.
known_limitations: Individual participation and eligible-day calculations require Bureau records.
researcher_notes: Statute and current regulation agree on the baseline rate.

text: A prisoner earns an additional five days of time credits for every thirty days of successful participation if the Bureau determines the prisoner to be at minimum or low risk for recidivating and, in the statute's words, the prisoner "over 2 consecutive assessments, has not increased their risk of recidivism"; the regulation words this condition differently, requiring that the inmate have "maintained a consistent minimum or low risk of recidivism over the most recent two consecutive risk and needs assessments." [18 U.S.C. § 3632(d)(4)(A)(ii)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3632); [28 C.F.R. § 523.42(c)(2)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title28-vol2/pdf/CFR-2025-title28-vol2-part523.pdf)
known_limitations: Individual PATTERN classifications and assessment dates require the record.
researcher_notes: Preserves the wording distinction between the statute and regulation. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: The statute bars credit for a program successfully completed before December 21, 2018 and for a program completed during official detention before the prisoner's sentence commences under § 3585(a).
known_limitations: The regulation separately controls its administrative earning start and historical transition.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of both clauses of § 3632(d)(4)(B).

text: The regulation allows an otherwise eligible inmate to earn for programming and activities from December 21, 2018 through January 14, 2020; beginning January 15, 2020, earning requires successful participation in programs or activities recommended from the individualized risk-and-needs assessment.
known_limitations: Actual historical awards depend on Bureau records and exclusions.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 523.42(b).

text: Under the regulation as amended effective September 30, 2026, an eligible inmate begins earning FSA Time Credits after the inmate's term of imprisonment commences; the amendment removed the former parenthetical that identified that date as the date the inmate arrives or voluntarily surrenders at the designated Bureau facility where the sentence will be served. [28 C.F.R. § 523.42(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-28/chapter-V/subchapter-B/part-523/subpart-E); [91 Fed. Reg. 55,740, 55,741, 55,743 (Aug. 31, 2026) (interim final rule)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-31/pdf/2026-17752.pdf)
known_limitations: Historical transition periods and individual designation facts must be checked separately.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 523.42(a). Re-reviewed 2026-10-15 against the sources listed in maintenance/legal-review-2026-10-15.md; wording approved by the owner. Revised 2026-10-30 after the legal-review recommendations, each checked against its source text; owner-approved.

text: Section 3632(d)(4)(D) makes a prisoner ineligible to earn FTCs when the prisoner is serving a sentence for a conviction under an enumerated provision; the current exact statutory list—not a category label or a fixed estimate of the number of offenses—controls the federal offense screen.
known_limitations: Aggregated sentences, prior-conviction provisions, and a particular judgment require separate analysis.
researcher_notes: Corrects the legacy's unverified fixed range of offense categories.

text: A final removal order is an application bar, not one of § 3632(d)(4)(D)'s earning exclusions: the regulation's earning rule excludes the enumerated-offense category, while § 3632(d)(4)(E) and § 523.44(a)(2) prohibit applying FTCs for a prisoner subject to a final order of removal.
known_limitations: A particular immigration order and its finality are factual and legal questions outside this module.
researcher_notes: Derived from the distinct statutory and regulatory earning and application provisions.

text: Section 3632(d)(4)(C) directs that earned FTCs be applied toward prerelease custody or supervised release and requires the Director to transfer eligible prisoners, as determined under § 3624(g); earning a credit and qualifying to apply it are therefore separate determinations. For supervised release, § 3624(g)(3) provides that the Director "may transfer" the prisoner to begin it early, "not to exceed 12 months," and a prisoner subject to a final order of removal is ineligible to apply time credits. [18 U.S.C. § 3632(d)(4)(C), (E)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3632); [18 U.S.C. § 3624(g)(1), (g)(3)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3624)
known_limitations: The claim does not decide whether an individual satisfies § 3624(g).
researcher_notes: Direct statutory cross-reference and structural distinction. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Before application, the prisoner must have credits equal to the remainder of the imposed term, must have demonstrated risk reduction or maintained minimum or low risk during imprisonment, and must have had the remainder of the term computed under applicable law.
known_limitations: Individual balances, risk history, and remainder computations require Bureau records.
researcher_notes: Nationwide general application gate.

text: For prerelease custody, § 3624(g) and § 523.44(c) additionally require minimum or low risk in the last two assessments, unless the warden approves the statutory petition after making the required danger, good-faith-effort, and recidivism findings.
known_limitations: A warden's findings and reviewability require the individual record and further authority.
researcher_notes: Prerelease-specific alternative gate.

text: Under the regulation, the Bureau may apply FTCs toward early transfer to supervised release only when the inmate meets the general application criteria in § 523.44(b) and the prerelease-custody criteria in § 523.44(c) (minimum or low risk through the last two assessments, or an approved warden petition), has maintained minimum or low risk through the last assessment, and has a court-imposed supervised-release term; the transfer may be no earlier than 12 months before it would otherwise have occurred. The statute likewise provides that the Director "may transfer" the prisoner to supervised release early, "not to exceed 12 months." [18 U.S.C. § 3624(g)(1)(D)(ii), (g)(3)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3624); [28 C.F.R. § 523.44(b)–(d)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title28-vol2/pdf/CFR-2025-title28-vol2-part523.pdf)
known_limitations: The sentencing judgment and Bureau calculation must be checked.
researcher_notes: Supervised-release-specific application gate and cap. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: An inmate may lose earned FTCs for violating program or activity requirements under Part 541 procedures, may seek review through the Bureau's Part 542 Administrative Remedy Program, and may receive case-specific restoration after clear conduct for two consecutive risk-and-needs assessments.
known_limitations: Part 541 procedure, Part 542 deadlines, and individual restoration decisions are not mapped here.
researcher_notes: Structural rule only; no exhaustion conclusion.

text: BOP Program Statement 5410.01, Change Notice 2, dated March 10, 2023, is official agency implementation policy for § 3632(d)(4); it does not displace the statute or regulation.
known_limitations: Nonbinding agency policy; individualized calculations and policy-law conflicts require separate review.
researcher_notes: Official BOP policy identity and hierarchy.

text: Section 2253(a) makes a final order in a district-court habeas proceeding subject to review in the court of appeals for the circuit in which the proceeding is held. Section 2253(b) allows no appeal from a final order in a proceeding to test the validity of a warrant to remove a person charged with a criminal offense against the United States to another district or place for commitment or trial, or of that person's detention pending removal proceedings, and § 2253(c)(1) requires a certificate of appealability for an appeal from the final order in a habeas proceeding arising out of state-court process or in a § 2255 proceeding. [28 U.S.C. § 2253(a)–(c)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/28/2253)
known_limitations: Section 2253(a) does not supply notice timing or resolve appealability of interlocutory orders.
researcher_notes: Direct paraphrase of § 2253(a). Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Section 2253(c)(1) requires a certificate of appealability only for a final habeas order in which the detention complained of arises from process issued by a state court, or for a final order in a § 2255 proceeding.
known_limitations: The classification must be applied to the actual source of the detention, not merely the petition label.
researcher_notes: Direct statutory two-category rule.

text: A federal-process § 2241 appeal that is not a § 2255 proceeding falls outside both categories in § 2253(c)(1), so § 2253 does not require a COA for that appeal.
known_limitations: No-COA status does not eliminate the notice of appeal, deadline, fee, or other appellate requirements.
researcher_notes: Negative implication from the exhaustive categories in § 2253(c)(1).

text: The same classification applies when a federal prisoner invokes § 2255(e)'s saving clause: § 2253(c)(1) imposes the certificate-of-appealability requirement only on state-process habeas and § 2255 final orders, and in *Bruce*, a saving-clause appeal, the Third Circuit stated that the § 2253(c) requirements do not apply to prisoners appealing the denial of a § 2241 petition. *Jones v. Hendrix* later held that the saving clause does not authorize the *Dorsainvil* statutory-claim pathway *Bruce* applied, so *Bruce* is cited here only for its certificate-of-appealability statement. [28 U.S.C. § 2253(c)(1)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/28/2253); [*Bruce*, 868 F.3d 170](https://www2.ca3.uscourts.gov/opinarch/144284p.pdf); [*Jones*, 599 U.S. at 477](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/22pdf/599us1r42_2b35.pdf)
known_limitations: Bruce is binding in the Third Circuit and illustrative elsewhere; § 2253(c)'s text supplies the nationwide classification. This claim does not establish saving-clause availability on the merits.
researcher_notes: Bruce itself was a saving-clause § 2241 appeal and states that § 2253(c) did not apply. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: When the detention complained of arises from state-court process, § 2253(c)(1)(A) requires a COA to appeal the final habeas order even if the petition was filed under § 2241.
known_limitations: The custody source must be determined from the record; physical confinement in a federal facility is not alone dispositive.
researcher_notes: Section 2253(c)(1)(A) turns on state-court process, not the statutory caption.

text: Rule 22(b)(3) separately says that a state, the United States, or their representative does not need a COA when that government actor appeals; subsection (b)(3) is not the source of the no-COA rule for a federal prisoner's § 2241 appeal.
known_limitations: Local circuit COA procedures remain to be checked where a COA is required.
researcher_notes: Corrects the legacy reliance on Rule 22(b)(3) for a prisoner appeal.

text: The absence of a COA requirement does not perfect an appeal. Rule 3 requires a notice of appeal filed with the district clerk, and Rule 4(a)(1) supplies a thirty-day default and a sixty-day period when a listed United States party, officer, or employee is a party; the actual parties and posture must be checked before calendaring.
known_limitations: The actual parties, judgment date, postjudgment motions, inmate-filing rule, and local practice must be checked before calculating a deadline.
researcher_notes: Current Rules 3(a)(1) and 4(a)(1); does not assign one universal § 2241 deadline.

text: Sections 2241(c)(3) and 2243 authorize custody-focused habeas relief; they do not independently create a substantive entitlement to credits, release, placement, or another benefit.
known_limitations: The specific remedy depends on the substantive source of law, the record, and controlling precedent.
researcher_notes: Statutory remedial boundary; § 2241 is a vehicle, not a standalone benefit statute.

text: For a state prisoner challenging the fact or duration of physical confinement and seeking immediate or speedier release, Preiser v. Rodriguez identifies habeas—not § 1983—as the sole federal remedy.
known_limitations: Preiser addressed state prisoners and the habeas-versus-§ 1983 boundary; it does not itself decide every federal-prisoner execution claim or remedy.
researcher_notes: Holding bounded to the opinion's procedural context.

text: For state-prisoner § 1983 claims, Wilkinson v. Dotson holds that a procedural challenge lies outside habeas's core when success would not necessarily spell immediate or speedier release, as where success produces only a new discretionary parole review.
known_limitations: The holding does not itself establish a Bivens or other cause of action against federal actors.
researcher_notes: Preserves the state-prisoner and § 1983 posture.

text: A successful saving-clause § 2241 petition therefore should not be described automatically as “functioning like” § 2255 with the same remedial menu; the particular relief requires claim-specific and controlling-circuit authority.
known_limitations: The exact relief available in a viable saving-clause case requires controlling-circuit authority and the substantive claim; this claim establishes only that the statutes do not contain identical remedial text.
researcher_notes: Side-by-side statutory comparison correcting an unsupported legacy equivalence.

text: When the Bureau retains statutory discretion but used an unlawful decision process, the habeas remedy may be lawful reconsideration rather than an order awarding the discretionary placement.
known_limitations: Binding only in the Ninth Circuit; the decision addressed a specific § 3621(b) designation error and does not establish a universal § 2241 remedy.
researcher_notes: Official published Ninth Circuit opinion, disposition at 823 F.3d 1243.

text: The available execution-of-sentence remedy consequently depends on the underlying statute, the proven entitlement, and whether the decisionmaker retains discretion. Recalculation, restoration, release, or reconsideration cannot be promised as interchangeable outcomes merely because the pleading invokes § 2241.
known_limitations: Rodriguez is a Ninth Circuit example; each substantive statute, circuit, and record must be independently researched.
researcher_notes: Bounded remedial synthesis, not a promise of a particular outcome.

text: Section 404(a) defines a covered offense as a violation of a federal criminal statute whose statutory penalties were modified by Fair Sentencing Act § 2 or § 3 and that was committed before August 3, 2010.
known_limitations: The actual statute and penalty provision of conviction must be identified.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: Fair Sentencing Act § 2 raised the crack quantities in 21 U.S.C. §§ 841(b)(1) and 960(b) from 5 to 28 grams for the lower mandatory-minimum tier and from 50 to 280 grams for the higher tier; § 3 removed the crack-specific mandatory-minimum sentence from 21 U.S.C. § 844(a).
known_limitations: Historical amendment summary; current individual penalties require the applicable statute and offense date.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: For a covered offense, the sentencing court may act on a motion by the defendant, the Bureau of Prisons Director, the attorney for the Government, or the court and may impose a reduced sentence as if Fair Sentencing Act §§ 2 and 3 had been in effect when the offense was committed.
known_limitations: Eligibility and authorization do not require a reduction.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: Section 404(c) bars the court from entertaining the motion if the sentence was previously imposed or reduced in accordance with the Fair Sentencing Act amendments, or if a previous § 404 motion was denied after December 21, 2018 following a complete review on the merits.
known_limitations: Application requires the actual prior order and record.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: Eligibility does not require a reduction: § 404(c) expressly preserves the court's discretion to deny or limit relief.
known_limitations: The court must still consider properly raised nonfrivolous arguments.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: Dorsey held that the Fair Sentencing Act's lower mandatory minimums apply to a pre-August 3, 2010 offender sentenced on or after that date.
known_limitations: Dorsey did not construe the later-enacted First Step Act § 404.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: Section 404 is not textually limited to defendants whose sentences were already final before August 3, 2010. Its definition turns on the offense date, the statute and statutory penalties, and the § 404(c) bars; Dorsey answers the separate pipeline question for pre-Act conduct followed by post-Act sentencing.
known_limitations: A post-Act sentence may independently trigger § 404(c); the text, not a historical shorthand, controls.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: Terry held that the Fair Sentencing Act did not modify the statutory penalties for the petitioner's 21 U.S.C. § 841(b)(1)(C) offense, whose statutory range remained unchanged, so that offense was not covered by § 404.
known_limitations: Does not resolve every mixed-count or sentencing-package issue.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: Covered-offense classification asks whether Fair Sentencing Act § 2 or § 3 modified the statutory penalties for the offense of conviction; a Guidelines change, sentencing conduct, or a crack-cocaine label alone does not satisfy § 404(a).
known_limitations: The Fair Sentencing Act also amended § 960(b), so hard-coded § 841-only screens are incomplete.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: Section 3582(c)(1)(B) is the gateway allowing a term of imprisonment to be modified when another statute expressly permits it; it adds no substantive or procedural limits of its own to a § 404 motion.
known_limitations: The authorizing statute's own limits still control.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: When deciding whether and how much to reduce a sentence under § 404, a district court may consider intervening changes of law or fact, including post-sentencing conduct and nonretroactive legal changes.
known_limitations: Consideration does not make the legal change retroactive or alter the benchmark range.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: The court must consider the parties' nonfrivolous arguments, but it may reject unpersuasive arguments without a detailed explanation and need provide only a brief statement of reasons.
known_limitations: Circuit-specific application to a particular order remains open.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: Concepcion does not require the court to reduce a sentence because of an intervening change or any other argument; it requires consideration, not persuasion or a particular result.
known_limitations: A legal calculation error remains distinct from the discretionary outcome.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: The benchmark Guidelines range may be recalculated only to reflect retroactive application of Fair Sentencing Act §§ 2 and 3. The court may then consider post-sentencing conduct or nonretroactive legal changes when selecting or rejecting a reduction, using the correctly calculated range as the benchmark.
known_limitations: Nonretroactive changes inform discretion but do not alter the benchmark range.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: *Concepcion* did not equate a § 404 proceeding with an original sentencing: the majority said only that "there are differences between the two," while holding that the only limits on the information a court may consider are those set by Congress in a statute or by the Constitution. That information rule is broad, but § 404(b)'s authorization, § 404(c)'s two explicit limitations, and the rule that the benchmark Guidelines range may be recalculated only to reflect the Fair Sentencing Act still control. [*Concepcion v. United States*, 597 U.S. 481 (2022)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/20-1650_new_4gci.pdf); [First Step Act of 2018, Pub. L. No. 115-391, § 404, 132 Stat. 5194, 5222](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-115publ391/pdf/PLAW-115publ391.pdf)
known_limitations: Hearing and presence rules require circuit-specific research.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Section 404(c) provides that no court shall entertain a motion made under § 404 to reduce a sentence if the sentence was previously imposed or previously reduced in accordance with the amendments made by sections 2 and 3 of the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010, or if a previous § 404 motion to reduce the sentence was, after the date of enactment of the First Step Act, denied after a complete review of the motion on the merits. Section 404 does not list a prior § 3582(c)(2) Guidelines reduction as a limitation; whether the first limitation applies depends on whether the sentence was previously imposed or previously reduced in accordance with the amendments made by sections 2 and 3 of the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010. [First Step Act of 2018, Pub. L. No. 115-391, § 404, 132 Stat. 5194, 5222](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-115publ391/pdf/PLAW-115publ391.pdf)
known_limitations: No conclusion about a particular prior order is possible without the record.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding. Corrected 2026-10-31 to follow the wording of the cited law or policy (owner directive); wording owner-approved 2026-10-31. Revised 2026-11-02 under the Nov. 1, 2026 double legal review, as checked against the saved sources; owner approved 2026-11-02; double legal review completed; licensed-attorney approval not recorded.

text: Section 404 itself states no filing deadline and no prior-request or administrative-exhaustion requirement; it authorizes the listed movants to proceed in the court that imposed the sentence.
known_limitations: Local filing procedures and standing orders remain open.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding.

text: Section 404(b) authorizes a reduced sentence only "as if sections 2 and 3 of the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 ... were in effect at the time the covered offense was committed," so a requested sentence must fit the penalties as those sections amended them or rest on a separately established legal basis; this follows from the "as if" text, since neither § 404 nor *Concepcion* addresses statutory minimums expressly. Section 404 does not make unrelated legal changes retroactive: the court need not recalculate the Guidelines "in any respect other than applying the Fair Sentencing Act," and postsentencing conduct or nonretroactive changes may inform only the choice of sentence, with the properly calculated range as the benchmark. [First Step Act of 2018, Pub. L. No. 115-391, § 404, 132 Stat. 5194, 5222](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-115publ391/pdf/PLAW-115publ391.pdf); [*Concepcion v. United States*, 597 U.S. 481 (2022)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/20-1650_new_4gci.pdf)
known_limitations: Independent safety-valve, substantial-assistance, or other authority must be established separately.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited statutory text or Supreme Court holding. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: For an arrest within the United States, Rule 5(a)(1)(A) requires the arresting person to take the defendant without unnecessary delay before a magistrate judge, or a qualifying state or local judicial officer under Rule 5(c), unless a statute provides otherwise. Rule 5(a)(2) excepts certain arrests on a complaint charging solely a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 1073, and provides that Rule 32.1 applies to an arrest for violating probation or supervised release and Rule 40 to an arrest for failing to appear in another district. The rule does not establish a 48-hour presentment threshold. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 5(a)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2025-02/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure-dec-1-2024.pdf)
known_limitations: The place and officer qualifications in Rule 5(c), and any statutory exception, remain material.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: The 48-hour framework in County of Riverside v. McLaughlin concerns the Fourth Amendment requirement of a prompt judicial probable-cause determination after a warrantless arrest. A determination within 48 hours generally satisfies promptness, although an arrested person may prove unreasonable delay; after 48 hours the government must show a bona fide emergency or other extraordinary circumstance.
known_limitations: The 48-hour framework is not a Rule 5 presentment deadline.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: For a federal confession, 18 U.S.C. § 3501(c) provides that a confession made within six hours of arrest (or a longer period reasonable considering the means of transportation and the distance to the nearest available magistrate judge) is not inadmissible solely because of presentment delay; within that window it is admissible, subject to the other Rules of Evidence, if made voluntarily. If the confession occurred before presentment and beyond six hours, the court must decide whether the delay was unreasonable or unnecessary under the McNabb–Mallory cases, and if it was, the confession is to be suppressed. [Corley v. United States, 556 U.S. 303, 322 (2009)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/556bv.pdf)
known_limitations: The holding concerns federal confession admissibility, not every remedy for presentment delay.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: After a warrantless arrest, a complaint satisfying Rule 4(a)'s probable-cause requirement must be promptly filed in the district where the offense allegedly occurred.
known_limitations: The claim does not determine whether a particular complaint established probable cause.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: Rule 5(c) determines the place and transfer procedure for the initial appearance. The ordinary location depends on whether the arrest occurred in the charging district, another district, or after extradition; the chart therefore cannot assume every arrest goes immediately before a magistrate in the charging district.
known_limitations: Identity, Rule 20, Rule 40, and extradition applications require their own facts and rules.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: In a felony case, Rule 5(d)(1) requires advice concerning: the complaint and any filed affidavit; retained or appointed counsel; circumstances for pretrial release; any preliminary-hearing right; the right not to make a statement and the possible use of a statement; and consular notification for a noncitizen.
known_limitations: Misdemeanor procedure follows Rule 5(e) and Rule 58 rather than this felony list.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: The judge must allow a reasonable opportunity to consult counsel and must release or detain the defendant as statutes and rules provide. Rule 5 itself does not make Sixth Amendment attachment a statutory trigger for a detention hearing.
known_limitations: This does not decide the Sixth Amendment critical-stage question for a particular hearing.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: A preliminary hearing is not required in every case. If a defendant is charged with an offense other than a petty offense, Rule 5.1(a) requires a magistrate judge to conduct a preliminary hearing unless the defendant waives the hearing; the defendant is indicted; the government files an information under Rule 7(b) charging the defendant with a felony; the government files an information charging the defendant with a misdemeanor; or the defendant is charged with a misdemeanor and consents to trial before a magistrate judge. Unless a magistrate judge extends the time limits under Rule 5.1(d), the magistrate judge must hold the preliminary hearing within a reasonable time, but no later than 14 days after the initial appearance if the defendant is in custody and no later than 21 days if not in custody. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 5.1(a), (c)–(d) (Dec. 1, 2025 ed.)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Extensions and the effect of later indictment require the actual docket and Rule 5.1.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding. Corrected 2026-10-31 to follow the wording of the cited law or policy (owner directive); wording owner-approved 2026-10-31. Revised 2026-11-02 under the Nov. 1, 2026 double legal review, as checked against the saved sources; owner approved 2026-11-02; double legal review completed; licensed-attorney approval not recorded.

text: Rothgery held that an initial appearance before a judicial officer at which the defendant learns the formal accusation and liberty is restricted initiates adversary judicial proceedings and triggers attachment of the Sixth Amendment right to counsel; prosecutor awareness or participation is not required.
known_limitations: Attachment does not itself decide whether counsel must be present at a particular postattachment event.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: Attachment and critical-stage analysis are distinct. Rothgery did not hold that attachment itself creates a § 3142 detention hearing, nor did it decide the scope of counsel's required presence at every postattachment proceeding; § 3142(f), not attachment, defines when a detention hearing is held.
known_limitations: The critical-stage status of a particular proceeding remains open.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: Section 3142(a) supplies four possible pretrial orders: release on personal recognizance or unsecured appearance bond; release on conditions; temporary detention under subsection (d); or detention under subsection (e).
known_limitations: The correct order depends on the remaining statutory subsections and record.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: Section 3142(b) makes recognizance or unsecured-bond release the starting rule unless the judicial officer determines that it will not reasonably assure appearance or will endanger another person or the community.
known_limitations: This is a starting rule, not an outcome when subsection (b)'s exception is found.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: If subsection (b) is insufficient, subsection (c) requires the least restrictive further condition or combination that will reasonably assure appearance and safety. A financial condition may not be imposed if it results in pretrial detention.
known_limitations: Condition selection is individualized and subject to the statute.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: On the government's motion, § 3142(f)(1) requires a detention hearing in a case that involves: a crime of violence, a § 1591 violation, or a listed terrorism offense with a maximum term of 10 years or more; an offense with a maximum sentence of life imprisonment or death; a qualifying drug offense with a maximum term of ten years or more; any felony if the person has been convicted of two or more offenses described in (A) through (C), or state or local equivalents, or a combination of such offenses; or any felony that is not otherwise a crime of violence that involves a minor victim, the possession or use of a firearm, destructive device, or any other dangerous weapon, or a § 2250 failure to register. [18 U.S.C. § 3142(f)(1)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3142)
known_limitations: The exact current statutory definitions and conviction record control.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: On the government's motion or the court's own motion, § 3142(f)(2) requires a hearing in a case involving a serious risk of flight or a serious risk that the person will obstruct or attempt to obstruct justice, or threaten, injure, or intimidate a prospective witness or juror.
known_limitations: The risks must be serious and supported by the individual record.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: A § 3142(f) category triggers a hearing to determine whether any condition or combination of conditions will reasonably assure appearance and safety, not mandatory detention. The hearing shall be held immediately upon the person's first appearance unless the person or the government seeks a continuance; except for good cause, a defense continuance may not exceed five days and a government continuance three days (not including any intermediate Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday), and the person shall be detained during a continuance. The person has the right to counsel, appointed if financially unable to obtain adequate representation, and an opportunity to testify, present witnesses, cross-examine witnesses who appear, and present information by proffer or otherwise; the rules concerning admissibility of evidence in criminal trials do not apply. [18 U.S.C. § 3142(e)(1), (f)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3142)
known_limitations: Circuit-specific evidence and proffer practices remain open.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: After the subsection (f) hearing, § 3142(e)(1) requires detention only if the judicial officer finds that no condition or combination will reasonably assure the person's appearance and the safety of another person and the community. Subsection (e)(1) is the detention rule; it is not a rebuttable-presumption category.
known_limitations: The necessary evidence and findings are case-specific.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: The facts supporting a detention finding based on inability to reasonably assure safety must be established by clear and convincing evidence. Section 3142(f) does not state the burden of proof for a flight-based detention finding, so this nationwide module does not assign one without controlling circuit authority.
known_limitations: The flight burden requires controlling circuit authority.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: Section 3142(e)(2) creates a safety-only rebuttable presumption in a subsection (f)(1) case only when the person has a described prior conviction, committed that prior offense while on pretrial release, and is within five years of the later of that conviction or release from imprisonment. It is not the ten-year-drug-offense presumption.
known_limitations: Every statutory prerequisite must be established from the record.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: Section 3142(e)(3) creates a rebuttable presumption concerning both appearance and safety upon probable cause for the specifically listed drug, firearm, terrorism, trafficking, and minor-victim offenses. A § 924(c) offense appears in this subsection, but the complete statutory list and thresholds control.
known_limitations: The exact charged offense and probable-cause basis control.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: Both statutory presumptions are subject to rebuttal. Their application does not itself produce an automatic detention order; the judicial officer must apply the statute's hearing, factors, and no-adequate-condition framework. The nationwide effect of rebuttal on the burdens of production and persuasion is not resolved here.
known_limitations: Circuit-specific burden allocation after rebuttal remains open.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding.

text: The § 3142(c) conditions menu includes third-party custody and restrictions on travel, associations, intoxicants, and controlled substances, among other options; it also permits any other reasonably necessary condition. Every release under § 3142(c) is subject to the no-new-crime condition and, where authorized, DNA-sample collection, and the judicial officer must otherwise impose the least restrictive further condition or combination of conditions that will reasonably assure appearance and safety, except that in a listed minor-victim case or a § 2250 failure-to-register case any release order shall contain, at a minimum, electronic monitoring and the conditions in subparagraphs (iv) through (viii). [18 U.S.C. § 3142(c)(1)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3142)
known_limitations: A particular monitoring or testing condition requires an individualized order and legal basis.
researcher_notes: Nationwide rule bounded to the cited current rule, statute, or Supreme Court holding. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Under § 3582(c), the court "may not modify a term of imprisonment once it has been imposed" except through subsection (c)(1)(A) (with separate routes in clauses (i) and (ii)), subsection (c)(1)(B), or subsection (c)(2); § 3582(b) separately recognizes correction under Rule 35 and § 3742 and appeal and modification under § 3742 if the sentence is outside the guideline range, and makes the judgment final "for all other purposes." Each door has different eligibility, procedure, and limits. [18 U.S.C. § 3582(b)–(c)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3582)
known_limitations: Claims outside these doors require an independently authorized remedy.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Subsections (a) and (b) govern imposition and finality, subsection (d) imposes specified Bureau of Prisons notice and assistance duties, and subsection (e) concerns certain nonassociation orders. None is an additional sentence-reduction door.
known_limitations: This claim does not adjudicate performance of any Bureau duty.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority.

text: *Fernandez* holds that the supposed invalidity of a conviction cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason under § 3582(c)(1)(A); § 2255 is Congress's designated collateral vehicle for a federal prisoner attacking conviction validity.
known_limitations: A fact may have a distinct permissible relevance that does not ask the § 3582 court to adjudicate conviction validity.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority.

text: Rule 35(a) authorizes the sentencing court to correct an arithmetical, technical, or other clear error within 14 days after sentencing; Rule 35(c) defines “sentencing” as the oral announcement of the sentence.
known_limitations: Whether a particular error is within Rule 35(a) requires the sentencing record.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority.

text: Rule 35(b) requires a government motion. A motion within one year of sentencing is governed by Rule 35(b)(1), which requires that the defendant, "after sentencing, provided substantial assistance in investigating or prosecuting another person"; a later motion must fit one of Rule 35(b)(2)'s three information-timing categories. Presentence assistance may be considered only in evaluating whether the defendant has provided substantial assistance, and the court "may" reduce the sentence, including to a level below a statutory minimum. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 35(b)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2025-02/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure-dec-1-2024.pdf)
known_limitations: Government-motion review and plea-agreement enforcement require separate authority and facts.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Rule 36 separately permits the court, after giving any notice it considers appropriate, to correct at any time a clerical error in a judgment, order, or other part of the record, or an error in the record arising from oversight or omission. Its text reaches only those errors, not a substantive resentencing, and it is not a § 3582(c) reduction door, because § 3582(c)(1)(B) refers only to statutes and Rule 35. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 36](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/2025-02/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure-dec-1-2024.pdf); [18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(B)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3582)
known_limitations: The oral and written record must be compared to classify the asserted error.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Section 3582(c)(1)(B) is a connector: it permits modification only to the extent Rule 35 or another statute expressly permits. The outside rule or statute supplies the movant, deadline, eligibility, scope, and discretionary limits.
known_limitations: Section 3582(c)(1)(B) alone does not create substantive eligibility.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority.

text: The Bureau of Prisons Director may move under § 3582(c)(1)(A). A defendant may move after fully exhausting administrative appeal of the Bureau's failure to file, or after 30 days from the warden's receipt of the defendant's request, whichever occurs first.
known_limitations: Issue exhaustion, waiver, forfeiture, and emergency applications require controlling circuit law.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority.

text: For the ordinary compassionate-release path, the court must consider the applicable § 3553(a) factors and find an extraordinary and compelling reason, consistency with the applicable Commission policy statement, and the policy statement's no-danger requirement. The court may reduce the prison term and, under the statute, "may impose a term of probation or supervised release with or without conditions that does not exceed the unserved portion of the original term of imprisonment"; § 1B1.13(a) refers only to supervised release. [18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3582); [U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(a) (2026)](https://www.ussc.gov/guidelines/2026-guidelines-manual/annotated-2026-chapter-1)
known_limitations: No individual eligibility, danger, discretion, or relief determination is made.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30. Corrected 2026-10-31 for the Guidelines amendments effective Nov. 1, 2026; wording owner-approved 2026-10-31.

text: The separate age-70 route in § 3582(c)(1)(A)(ii) requires age 70 or older, at least 30 years served on a sentence imposed under 18 U.S.C. § 3559(c) for the offense or offenses of current imprisonment, and a Bureau of Prisons determination that the defendant is not a danger. Like the ordinary route, it also requires a motion by the Director or by the defendant after exhaustion or the lapse of 30 days, consideration of the § 3553(a) factors, and consistency with § 1B1.13, including the court's own no-danger determination under § 1B1.13(a)(2); it is not the ordinary age-based circumstance in § 1B1.13(b)(2). [18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A)(ii)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3582); [U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(a), (b)(2) (2026)](https://www.ussc.gov/guidelines/2026-guidelines-manual/annotated-2026-chapter-1)
known_limitations: Every statutory element requires the individual record.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30. Corrected 2026-10-31 for the Guidelines amendments effective Nov. 1, 2026; wording owner-approved 2026-10-31.

text: The current policy statement says extraordinary and compelling reasons exist under any of the circumstances in § 1B1.13(b) "or a combination thereof": medical circumstances, age, family circumstances, victim of abuse, other reasons similar in gravity (considered by themselves or together with reasons in (b)(1) through (4)), and an unusually long sentence under (b)(6), which remains printed but which *Rutherford* holds invalid to the extent it counsels that Congress's nonretroactive change to § 924(c), considered by itself or in combination with other factors, can make a prisoner eligible. The victim-of-abuse category requires that the defendant, while in custody serving the term of imprisonment sought to be reduced, was a victim of sexual abuse involving a "sexual act" or physical abuse resulting in "serious bodily injury," committed by, or at the direction of, a correctional officer, an employee or contractor of the Federal Bureau of Prisons, or any other individual who had custody or control over the defendant, with the misconduct established by a conviction, a civil finding or admission of liability, or an administrative finding unless those proceedings are unduly delayed or the defendant is in imminent danger; sympathy or seriousness alone is not a category. [U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b) (2026)](https://www.ussc.gov/guidelines/2026-guidelines-manual/annotated-2026-chapter-1); [*Rutherford v. United States*, 608 U.S. ___ (2026)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-820_97be.pdf)
known_limitations: The module does not determine whether particular facts meet a category.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority. text: *Rutherford* holds that when Congress declines to make a sentencing amendment retroactive, the resulting disparity cannot serve as an extraordinary and compelling reason under § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i). Congress's nonretroactive change to § 924(c), "considered by itself or in combination with other factors," cannot make a prisoner eligible for compassionate release. [*Rutherford v. United States*, 608 U.S. ___ (2026)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-820_97be.pdf)
known_limitations: The holding concerns deliberate statutory nonretroactivity rather than every later legal development.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: A federal prisoner who collaterally attacks the validity of his conviction "must proceed through 28 U.S.C. § 2255, not 18 U.S.C. § 3582"; "the supposed invalidity of a conviction is not among the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' that justify compassionate release" under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A). Whether a motion challenges a conviction "turns on the nature of the arguments presented," even if the prisoner does not ask to have the conviction vacated or set aside. *Fernandez* also held that a compassionate-release motion is not a vehicle for raising an actual-innocence claim. It left open whether a freestanding actual-innocence claim may be brought under § 2255. [*Fernandez v. United States*, 608 U.S. 411, 415, 423, 427–428, 430 (2026)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/608us2r39_5iek.pdf)
known_limitations: States Fernandez's rule for challenges to the validity of a conviction only; the opinion does not extend it to sentence challenges, and it leaves open whether a freestanding actual-innocence claim is cognizable under § 2255.
researcher_notes: Added 2026-11-02: new claim proposed by the Nov. 1, 2026 double legal review; wording checked against the saved U.S. Reports version (608 U.S. 411); owner approved 2026-11-02; double legal review completed; licensed-attorney approval not recorded.

text: Section 3582(c)(2) applies to a defendant sentenced based on a sentencing range that the Commission later lowered under 28 U.S.C. § 994(o), when a reduction is consistent with applicable Commission policy. The defendant or Bureau Director may move, and the court may act on its own motion; the compassionate-release warden-request gate does not apply.
known_limitations: Eligibility and extent still depend on § 1B1.10 and the actual sentencing framework.

text: Eligibility requires an amendment listed in current § 1B1.10(d) and an actual lowering of the defendant's applicable guideline range. An amendment's effective date or favorable treatment at new sentencings does not by itself make it retroactive under § 3582(c)(2). [18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(2)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3582); [U.S.S.G. § 1B1.10(a), (d) (2026)](https://www.ussc.gov/guidelines/2026-guidelines-manual/annotated-2026-chapter-1)

text: A Rule 11(c)(1)(C) agreement does not automatically defeat § 3582(c)(2) eligibility. Under *Hughes*, the sentence is based on the guideline range when that range was part of the framework the court relied on in imposing sentence or accepting the agreement.

text: *Dillon* establishes a two-step inquiry. First, the court determines whether and to what extent § 1B1.10 authorizes a reduction; second, if a reduction is authorized, the court considers applicable § 3553(a) factors and decides whether the authorized reduction is warranted.
known_limitations: The first-step limit cannot be bypassed at the discretionary step.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority.

text: At step one, the court substitutes only the listed amendment and leaves all other guideline-application decisions unaffected. A § 3582(c)(2) proceeding does not impose a new sentence in the usual sense and is not a plenary resentencing. United States*, 560 U.S. 817, 825–31 (2010)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-560/pdf/USREPORTS-560-817.pdf)

text: In a criminal case, Rule 4(b)(1)(A) requires a defendant's notice of appeal to be filed in the district court within 14 days after the later of the entry of the judgment or order being appealed or the filing of the government's notice of appeal, and Rule 3(a)(1) requires filing the notice with the district clerk. For an appeal from a judgment of conviction, a timely motion listed in Rule 4(b)(3)(A) (judgment of acquittal under Rule 29, new trial under Rule 33, or arrest of judgment under Rule 34, with a new-trial motion based on newly discovered evidence counting only if made no later than 14 days after entry of the judgment) moves the deadline to 14 days after entry of the order disposing of the last such motion, or after entry of the judgment of conviction if later, and an inmate's notice can be timely under Rule 4(c)(1) if it meets that rule's deposit conditions. [Fed. R. App. P. 3(a)(1), 4(b)(1)(A), (b)(3)(A), (c)(1)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-appellate-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The actual order, entry date, party, and deadline-affecting events must be checked.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Rule 4(c) governs timely inmate filing, and Rule 4(b)(4) allows the district court, upon good cause or excusable neglect, to extend the criminal appeal period by no more than 30 days from the original deadline. The possible extension is not part of the ordinary filing period.
known_limitations: Application requires the actual deposit, declaration, deadline, and district-court finding.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current text and controlling Supreme Court authority.

text: Federal constitutional law does not require prosecutors to file charges as soon as probable cause exists. *Lovasco* permits good-faith investigative delay while prosecutors complete an investigation and decide whether they can and should prosecute.
known_limitations: Investigative methods, charging motive, and agency authority require separate law.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: Rule 3 defines a complaint as a written statement of the essential facts constituting the charged offense. Except for Rule 4.1's electronic procedure, it must be made under oath before a magistrate judge or, if none is reasonably available, a state or local judicial officer.
known_limitations: Rule 4.1 supplies the electronic-procedure exception.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: Under Rule 4(a), a complaint and any supporting affidavits must establish probable cause to believe both that an offense was committed and that the defendant committed it. The judge then must issue a warrant, or at a government attorney's request must issue a summons instead.
known_limitations: Application requires the complaint and supporting affidavits.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: Rule 4 requires a warrant to identify the defendant with reasonable certainty, describe the charged offense, command arrest and prompt presentation, and bear the judge's signature; a summons uses the same form but commands appearance at a stated time and place. Execution, service, and return follow Rule 4(c).
known_limitations: Application requires the actual warrant or summons and return.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: A person making an arrest within the United States must take the defendant without unnecessary delay before a magistrate judge, or before a state or local judicial officer as Rule 5(c) provides, unless a statute provides otherwise, and subject to the exceptions in Rule 5(a)(2). When a defendant appears in response to a summons under Rule 4, a magistrate judge must proceed under Rule 5(d) or (e), as applicable. Rule 5(c) governs the place of the initial appearance and transfer to another district. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 5(a), (c)–(e) (Dec. 1, 2025 ed.)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The detailed presentment and detention framework is in the linked pretrial module.

text: When the initial appearance occurs outside the alleged-offense district, Rule 5(c)(3)(D) requires the magistrate judge to transfer the defendant if the government produces the warrant, a certified copy of the warrant, or a reliable electronic form of either, and the judge finds that the defendant is the same person named in the indictment, information, or warrant. If the defendant was arrested without a warrant, Rule 5(c)(3)(B) requires the district court where the offense was allegedly committed to first issue a warrant before the transfer, and Rule 5(c)(3)(C) requires a preliminary hearing if Rule 5.1 requires it. The rule supplies an identity finding, not a universally separate proceeding labeled an “identity hearing.” [Fed. R. Crim. P. 5(c)(3)(B)–(D)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The record and any contested-identity procedure require district and circuit law.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: If a defendant is charged with an offense other than a petty offense, Rule 5.1(a) requires a magistrate judge to conduct a preliminary hearing unless the defendant waives the hearing; the defendant is indicted; the government files an information under Rule 7(b) charging the defendant with a felony; the government files an information charging the defendant with a misdemeanor; or the defendant is charged with a misdemeanor and consents to trial before a magistrate judge. If the hearing is held, the magistrate judge decides whether there is probable cause to believe an offense has been committed and the defendant committed it. If the magistrate judge finds no probable cause, the magistrate judge must dismiss the complaint and discharge the defendant, and a discharge does not preclude the government from later prosecuting the defendant for the same offense. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 5.1(a), (e)–(f) (Dec. 1, 2025 ed.)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Timing extensions and individual probable cause require the record.

text: The Fifth Amendment generally requires a grand-jury presentment or indictment before a person may be held to answer for a capital or otherwise infamous crime, subject to the amendment's land-or-naval-forces and militia exception.
known_limitations: The constitutional exception and offense classification control.
