text: Rule 6(a) requires a federal grand jury to have 16 to 23 members.
known_limitations: Juror qualification challenges require additional law.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: While the grand jury is in session, Rule 6(d) permits government attorneys, the witness being questioned, needed interpreters, and a court reporter or recording-device operator to be present; during deliberation and voting, only jurors and any interpreter needed for an impaired juror may be present.
known_limitations: No case-specific presence violation or remedy is decided.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: Except during deliberation and voting, Rule 6(e)(1) requires recording of grand-jury proceedings, but an unintentional recording failure does not invalidate a prosecution. Rule 6(e)(2) imposes secrecy on the listed participants and recipients; it does not authorize a court to impose a blanket secrecy obligation on every person.
known_limitations: Disclosure exceptions and remedies require the exact request and record.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: A grand jury may indict only with at least 12 jurors concurring, and the grand jury or its foreperson or deputy must return the indictment to a magistrate judge in open court, subject to the rule's video-return provision.
known_limitations: No challenge to a particular concurrence record is resolved.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: A magistrate judge may direct that a returned indictment remain secret until the defendant is in custody or released pending trial; the clerk then seals it, and disclosure is limited as Rule 6(e)(4) provides.

text: Rule 7(a) requires an indictment for an offense other than criminal contempt if the offense is punishable by death or imprisonment for more than one year; an offense punishable by one year or less may be prosecuted under Rule 58(b)(1).
known_limitations: The authorized misdemeanor procedure requires Rule 58 and the offense penalty.

text: Rule 7(a)(1) requires indictment for an offense (other than criminal contempt) punishable by death or by imprisonment for more than one year, but under Rule 7(b) an offense punishable by imprisonment for more than one year may be prosecuted by information if the defendant, in open court and after being advised of the nature of the charge and of the defendant's rights, waives prosecution by indictment. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 7(a)(1), (b)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)

text: After indictment, Rule 9 requires a warrant for each named defendant or, at the government's request, a summons; for a defendant named only in an information, accompanying affidavits must establish probable cause. The first appearance then proceeds under Rule 5.

text: Rule 7 and 18 U.S.C. §§ 3281, 3282, 3288, and 3289 do not mention superseding indictments or state any “relation back” rule for them. A later charge of an offense (other than criminal contempt) punishable by death or by imprisonment for more than one year must still be prosecuted by indictment under Rule 7(a)(1); under Rule 7(b), an offense punishable by imprisonment for more than one year may be prosecuted by information if the defendant, in open court and after being advised of the nature of the charge and of the defendant's rights, waives prosecution by indictment. For a non-capital offense, § 3282(a) sets the general rule that, except as otherwise expressly provided by law, no person shall be prosecuted, tried, or punished unless the indictment is found or the information is instituted within five years after the offense was committed; these texts do not say how that period applies to a superseding indictment, so its timeliness must be determined from sources outside them. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 7(a)(1), (b)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf); [18 U.S.C. § 3281](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3281?link-type=html); [18 U.S.C. § 3282(a)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title18/pdf/USCODE-2024-title18-partII-chap213.pdf); [18 U.S.C. § 3288](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3288?link-type=html); [18 U.S.C. § 3289](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3289?link-type=html)
known_limitations: The exact timeliness test requires controlling circuit law and comparison of the charges.

text: An indictment for an offense punishable by death may be found at any time without limitation under 18 U.S.C. § 3281.

text: Except as otherwise expressly provided by law, § 3282(a) requires an indictment to be found or an information instituted within five years after a noncapital offense was committed.
known_limitations: Expressly different statutes and accrual doctrine may displace the default.

text: The five-year period in § 3282(a) is a default: it applies “[e]xcept as otherwise expressly provided by law,” covers only offenses “not capital,” and runs from when the offense “shall have been committed.” Section 3281 allows an indictment for any offense punishable by death to be found at any time without limitation, and under § 3282(b) an indictment for a chapter 109A offense that describes an accused whose name is unknown by a particular DNA profile, if found within five years after the offense, is not subject to the subsection (a) limitations period. [18 U.S.C. § 3282(a)–(b)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title18/pdf/USCODE-2024-title18-partII-chap213.pdf); [18 U.S.C. § 3281](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3281?link-type=html)
known_limitations: Specific limitation, tolling, and completion rules remain open until the offense and facts are known.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Under § 3288, when an indictment or information charging a felony is dismissed for any reason after the applicable limitations period has expired, a new indictment may be returned in the appropriate jurisdiction within six calendar months of the date of dismissal; within 60 days of the date the dismissal becomes final, in the event of an appeal; or, if no regular grand jury is in session there when the charge is dismissed, within six calendar months of the date the next regular grand jury is convened. The section does not permit a new indictment or information where the reason for the dismissal was the failure to file within the limitations period or some other reason that would bar a new prosecution. [18 U.S.C. § 3288](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3288?link-type=html)
known_limitations: Application requires dismissal timing, reason, appeal, and grand-jury facts.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Section 3289 supplies a related refiling window when an indictment or information charging a felony is dismissed for any reason before the applicable limitations period has expired and that period will expire within six calendar months of the dismissal: a new indictment may be returned within six calendar months of the expiration of the limitations period (not of the dismissal); within 60 days of the date the dismissal becomes final, in the event of an appeal; or, if no regular grand jury is in session in the appropriate jurisdiction when the limitations period expires, within six calendar months of the date the next regular grand jury is convened. It too does not permit a new indictment or information where the reason for the dismissal was the failure to file within the limitations period or some other reason that would bar a new prosecution. [18 U.S.C. § 3289](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3289?link-type=html)
known_limitations: Application requires dismissal timing, reason, appeal, and grand-jury facts.

text: Section 3161(b) requires that any information or indictment charging an individual with the commission of an offense be filed within 30 days from the date on which the individual was arrested or served with a summons in connection with the charges. If the individual has been charged with a felony in a district in which no grand jury has been in session during that 30-day period, the period of time for filing the indictment is extended an additional 30 days. Under § 3161(h), the periods of delay listed there are excluded in computing the time within which an information or an indictment must be filed. [18 U.S.C. § 3161(b), (h)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3161)
known_limitations: The actual clock is subject to § 3161(h) and the arrest-or-summons connection requirement.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open. text: In any case in which a plea of not guilty is entered, § 3161(c)(1) requires that the trial of a defendant charged in an information or indictment commence within 70 days from the filing date (and making public) of the information or indictment, or from the date the defendant has appeared before a judicial officer of the court in which the charge is pending, whichever date last occurs. Under § 3161(h), the periods of delay listed there are excluded in computing the time within which the trial must commence. [18 U.S.C. § 3161(c)(1), (h)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3161)
known_limitations: The actual clock requires the plea, public filing, appearance, and full docket.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open. text: The Speedy Trial Act is not computed by simply counting 30 or 70 calendar days: § 3161(h) excludes specified periods, and the actual calculation must use the docket, each exclusion, and any findings required for an ends-of-justice continuance.
known_limitations: Each exclusion and required finding must be established from the docket.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: If the § 3161(b) charging period, as extended by § 3161(h), is violated, § 3162(a)(1) requires the complaint charge to be dismissed or otherwise dropped. If the § 3161(c) trial period, as extended by § 3161(h), is violated, § 3162(a)(2) requires dismissal of the indictment or information on the defendant's motion; the defendant has the burden of proof supporting the motion, the government has the burden of going forward with the evidence on any exclusion of time under § 3161(h)(3), and failure to move before trial or entry of a guilty or nolo plea waives that statutory dismissal right. In either setting, the statute lists factors the court must consider in deciding dismissal with or without prejudice. [18 U.S.C. § 3161(b)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3161); [18 U.S.C. § 3162(a)(1)–(2)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3162?link-type=html)
known_limitations: With-or-without-prejudice and motion-waiver applications are case-specific.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: The Sixth Amendment Speedy Trial Clause applies only after a person becomes an accused through formal indictment or information or the actual restraints of arrest and holding to answer a criminal charge; it does not govern the preceding investigative interval. Statutes of limitation are the primary safeguard against stale preaccusation charges.
known_limitations: Postaccusation Sixth Amendment delay and statutory clocks require separate analysis.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: The Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause has a limited role in preaccusation delay. Actual prejudice is generally necessary but not sufficient; the reasons for delay also matter, and good-faith investigative delay is not unconstitutional merely because the defense was somewhat prejudiced.
known_limitations: Circuit formulations and the actual reasons and prejudice evidence remain open.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: Article III requires a federal criminal trial in the state where the crime was committed, subject to Congress's rule for crimes outside any state; the Sixth Amendment requires a jury from the state and district where the crime was committed. Rule 18 requires prosecution in a district where the offense was committed unless a statute or the rules permit otherwise, and requires the court to set the place of trial within the district with due regard for the convenience of the defendant, any victim, and the witnesses, and the prompt administration of justice. [U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 3](https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/article-3/section-2/clause-3/); [U.S. Const. amend. VI](https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-6/); [Fed. R. Crim. P. 18](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The offense elements and any contrary statute determine the correct district.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Unless Congress expressly provides otherwise, § 3237(a) permits prosecution in any district where a federal offense begun in one district and completed in another, or committed in more than one district, was begun, continued, or completed; it also supplies a specific continuing-offense rule for mail, interstate or foreign transportation, and importation offenses. Notwithstanding subsection (a), § 3237(b) lets a defendant prosecuted in a district other than the one where the defendant resides, for an offense described in Internal Revenue Code § 7203, or for an offense described in § 7201 or § 7206(1), (2), or (5) (whether or not also described in another provision of law) where venue rests solely on a mailing to the Internal Revenue Service, elect, by motion filed in the district where the prosecution was begun, to be tried in the district where the defendant resided when the alleged offense was committed, if the motion is filed within twenty days after arraignment on the indictment or information. [18 U.S.C. § 3237(a)–(b)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3237)
known_limitations: Offense-specific enactments and conduct elements control application.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: When a conviction is reversed because trial occurred in the wrong venue or before a jury drawn from the wrong district, *Smith* holds that the Constitution permits retrial in the proper venue; the venue error does not itself require a judgment barring reprosecution.
known_limitations: The holding does not decide whether venue was proper or whether another bar prevents retrial.
researcher_notes: Nationwide organization claim bounded to official current primary sources; case-specific and circuit-sensitive applications remain open.

text: Rule 10 requires an arraignment in open court at which the court ensures that the defendant has the indictment or information, reads it or states the substance of the charge, and asks the defendant to plead. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 10(a)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The actual charging document and arraignment record control.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Under Rule 10(b), a defendant charged by indictment or misdemeanor information need not be present at arraignment if the defendant, in a written waiver signed by both the defendant and defense counsel, has waived appearance and affirmed receipt of the charging document and that the plea is not guilty, and the court accepts the waiver. Rule 43(b) separately excuses presence for an organization represented by counsel who is present and, for an offense punishable by fine or imprisonment of not more than one year, or both, when the court, with the defendant's written consent, permits arraignment by video teleconferencing or in the defendant's absence. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 10(b)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf); [Fed. R. Crim. P. 43(a)–(b)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The rule does not authorize waiver outside its charged-document and signature conditions.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Rule 10(c) permits arraignment by video teleconference only with the defendant's consent. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 10(c)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The record must establish consent.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Rule 16(a)(1) creates specified government-disclosure duties upon a defendant's request; it is not a general command to open every government file. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(a)(1)–(2)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Constitutional, statutory, local, and court-ordered duties remain separate.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: The statement provisions distinguish a relevant oral statement made in known-agent interrogation that the government intends to use at trial from the broader specified written, recorded, recorded-oral, and grand-jury statements covered by Rule 16(a)(1)(B). [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(a)(1)(A)–(B)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Each statement category has distinct interrogation, intent-to-use, possession, and knowledge conditions.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: On request and subject to the rule's possession, knowledge, materiality, intended-use, and ownership conditions, Rule 16(a)(1) also covers the defendant's prior record, documents and objects, examination and test reports, and expert-witness information. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(a)(1)(D)–(G)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The request and each category's rule-text conditions must be proved.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: For Rule 16 expert disclosures, the court by order or local rule must set a time sufficiently before trial to give the opposing side a fair opportunity to meet the evidence, and the current rule specifies the required opinions, bases, reasons, qualifications, prior publications, prior testimony, approval, signature, and supplementation information. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(a)(1)(G), (b)(1)(C)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The controlling court order or local rule supplies the actual disclosure date.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Except as permitted by Rule 16(a)(1)(A)–(D), (F), and (G), Rule 16(a)(2) does not authorize the discovery or inspection of reports, memoranda, or other internal government documents made by an attorney for the government or other government agent in connection with investigating or prosecuting the case. Rule 16(a)(2) also does not authorize the discovery or inspection of statements made by prospective government witnesses except as provided in 18 U.S.C. § 3500. Under Rule 16(a)(3), Rule 16 does not apply to the discovery or inspection of a grand jury's recorded proceedings, except as provided in Rules 6, 12(h), 16(a)(1), and 26.2. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(a)(2)–(3)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf); [18 U.S.C. § 3500](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: Independent constitutional and Rule 26.2 duties are not decided by the Rule 16 exclusion.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary. Corrected 2026-10-31 to follow the wording of the cited law or policy (owner directive); wording owner-approved 2026-10-31.

text: The defendant's reciprocal duties arise only under the conditions stated in Rule 16(b): the document duty applies, upon government request, if the defendant requested disclosure under Rule 16(a)(1)(E) and the government complied, and the report duty applies, upon government request, if the defendant requested disclosure under Rule 16(a)(1)(F) and the government complied, and in either case only for items within the defendant's possession, custody, or control that the defendant intends to use in the defendant's case-in-chief at trial or, for a report, that relate to the testimony of the witness who prepared it, if the defendant intends to call that witness; the expert-disclosure duty applies at the government's request, for expert testimony the defendant intends to use during the defendant's case-in-chief at trial, if the defendant requested disclosure under Rule 16(a)(1)(G) and the government complied, or if the defendant has given notice under Rule 12.2(b) of an intent to present expert testimony on the defendant's mental condition. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(b)(1)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The actual request, government compliance, intended use, and possession control.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Rule 16(c) imposes a continuing duty to disclose newly discovered evidence or material before or during trial when it is subject to Rule 16 and the opposing party previously requested, or the court ordered, production. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(c)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The item must remain within Rule 16 and have been requested or ordered.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: For good cause, Rule 16(d)(1) permits a court to deny, restrict, or defer discovery, or grant other appropriate relief, including on an ex parte written showing whose complete text the court must preserve under seal if relief is granted. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(d)(1)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Privileges, classified information, victim protection, and local sealing law require separate authority.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: For a Rule 16 violation, the court may order discovery on just terms, grant a continuance, prohibit use of undisclosed evidence, or enter another order just under the circumstances; the rule does not make one sanction automatic for every violation. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(d)(2)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: Appellate standards and case-specific sanction selection require controlling circuit law.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: No later than 14 days after arraignment, Rule 16.1(a) requires government and defense counsel to confer and try to agree on a timetable and procedures for Rule 16 disclosure; after that conference, either or both may ask the court to determine or modify disclosure arrangements. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16.1](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)
known_limitations: The actual arraignment date, computation, extensions, and court orders control.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Rule 45(a) supplies federal criminal time computation for periods in the rules, local rules, court orders, and statutes that do not specify a method; under Rule 45(b)(1), the court on its own may extend the time, or for good cause may do so on a party's motion made before the time expires or, after it expires, if the party failed to act because of excusable neglect. Rule 16.1 is not within Rule 45(b)(2)'s exception, which covers only action under Rule 35. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 45(a)–(b)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title18/pdf/USCODE-2024-title18-app.pdf)
known_limitations: No jurisdictional characterization is made; an actual extension requires the rule's showing and an order.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Rule 16, the Jencks Act, and the *Brady* line are separate sources with different triggers and coverage, so an item may require independent classification under more than one source rather than treatment under a single generic “discovery” rule. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 16](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf); [18 U.S.C. § 3500](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500); [*Brady v. Maryland*, 373 U.S. 83, 86–88 (1963)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-373/pdf/USREPORTS-373-83.pdf)
known_limitations: Overlap does not erase any source's distinct trigger, scope, or remedy.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: A true *Brady* violation has three components: evidence favorable to the accused, suppression by the government willfully or inadvertently, and resulting prejudice. [*Strickler v. Greene*, 527 U.S. 263, 281–82 (1999)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-527/pdf/USREPORTS-527-263.pdf); [*Brady*, 373 U.S. at 87](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-373/pdf/USREPORTS-373-83.pdf)
known_limitations: Application requires the complete record and the allegedly suppressed evidence.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Evidence may be favorable because it is exculpatory or because it impeaches a prosecution witness; impeachment evidence is not categorically outside the constitutional disclosure rule. [*Strickler*, 527 U.S. at 281–82](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-527/pdf/USREPORTS-527-263.pdf); [*United States v. Bagley*, 473 U.S. 667, 676–78 (1985)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-473/pdf/USREPORTS-473-667.pdf)
known_limitations: Favorability and materiality remain case-specific.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: The constitutional disclosure duty is not eliminated by the absence of a specific defense request: in Part III of *Bagley*, Justice Blackmun, joined only by Justice O'Connor, found the materiality standard sufficiently flexible to cover no-request, general-request, and specific-request nondisclosure, and Justice White's concurrence for three Justices agreed it covers all instances of prosecutorial failure to disclose favorable evidence. [*United States v. Bagley*, 473 U.S. 667, 682–83 (1985) (opinion of Blackmun, J.)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-473/pdf/USREPORTS-473-667.pdf); [*id.* at 685 (White, J., concurring in part and concurring in the judgment)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-473/pdf/USREPORTS-473-667.pdf)
known_limitations: A request may still matter to suppression, notice, remedies, and local procedure.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: The prosecution's good faith does not defeat a *Brady* claim, because suppression may be willful or inadvertent; prejudice and the other constitutional components remain required. [*Brady*, 373 U.S. at 87](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-373/pdf/USREPORTS-373-83.pdf); [*Strickler*, 527 U.S. at 281–82](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-527/pdf/USREPORTS-527-263.pdf)
known_limitations: Good faith does not eliminate the claim, but favorability, suppression, and prejudice remain required.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: Under *Bagley*, suppressed favorable evidence is material only if there is a reasonable probability that, had it been disclosed to the defense, the result of the proceeding would have been different; a reasonable probability is a probability sufficient to undermine confidence in the outcome. This formulation appears in Justice Blackmun's Part III opinion, joined only by Justice O'Connor, and was adopted by Justice White's three-Justice concurrence. [*United States v. Bagley*, 473 U.S. 667, 682 (1985) (opinion of Blackmun, J.)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-473/pdf/USREPORTS-473-667.pdf); [*id.* at 685 (White, J., concurring in part and concurring in the judgment)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-473/pdf/USREPORTS-473-667.pdf)
known_limitations: The standard must be applied to the complete case and requested remedy.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: *Kyles* requires materiality to be assessed collectively, not item by item, and makes clear that the inquiry is not a sufficiency-of-the-remaining-evidence test or a constitutional open-file mandate. [*Kyles v. Whitley*, 514 U.S. 419, 434–37 (1995)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-514/pdf/USREPORTS-514-419.pdf)
known_limitations: The prosecution's broader ethical or policy duties are not equated with the constitutional minimum.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: The individual prosecutor must learn of favorable evidence known to others acting on the government's behalf in the case, including police, but determining who falls within that case-specific group requires the actual investigative relationships and controlling law. [*Kyles*, 514 U.S. at 437–38](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-514/pdf/USREPORTS-514-419.pdf)
known_limitations: Case-specific team boundaries require investigative facts and controlling circuit law.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: *Giglio* treats an undisclosed promise of nonprosecution to a key government witness as credibility evidence within the due-process rule when the witness's reliability may determine guilt or innocence; it does not require a new trial for every item that might have been useful to the defense. [*Giglio v. United States*, 405 U.S. 150, 153–55 (1972)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-405/pdf/USREPORTS-405-150.pdf)
known_limitations: Not every useful credibility item is automatically material.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: For the promise at issue in *Giglio*, the prosecutor's office was treated as the government entity, so a promise by one assistant was attributable to the government despite the trial prosecutor's lack of personal knowledge. [*Giglio*, 405 U.S. at 154](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-405/pdf/USREPORTS-405-150.pdf)
known_limitations: The holding is bounded to the prosecutor's office and the promise at issue.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: The distinct *Napue* rule forbids the government from knowingly using false testimony or allowing known false testimony to go uncorrected, including falsehoods bearing on witness credibility; the materiality question asks whether there is any reasonable likelihood that the false testimony could have affected the jury's judgment. [*Napue v. Illinois*, 360 U.S. 264, 269–72 (1959)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-360/pdf/USREPORTS-360-264.pdf); [*Giglio*, 405 U.S. at 153–54](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-405/pdf/USREPORTS-405-150.pdf)
known_limitations: Knowledge, falsity, correction, and reasonable likelihood require record-specific proof.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: In a federal criminal prosecution, § 3500(a) bars subpoena, discovery, or inspection of any statement or report in United States possession made by a government witness or prospective government witness (other than the defendant) until that witness has testified on direct examination in the trial of the case. [18 U.S.C. § 3500(a)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: Independent constitutional obligations must be classified separately.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: After a witness called by the United States testifies on direct, § 3500(b) requires the court, on the defendant's motion, to order the United States to produce any statement of the witness in its possession that relates to the subject matter of the testimony. When a statement is delivered, § 3500(c) provides that the court in its discretion, upon the defendant's application, may recess proceedings for the time reasonably required to examine the statement and prepare for its use. [18 U.S.C. § 3500(b)–(c)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: Possession, statement status, relation to testimony, and a motion must be established.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: If the United States claims that a statement contains matter unrelated to the witness's testimony, § 3500(c) requires in camera inspection, excision of unrelated portions, and delivery of the remainder to the defendant. If any portion is withheld, the defendant objects, and the trial is continued to an adjudication of guilt, the entire text of the statement shall be preserved by the United States and, in the event the defendant appeals, made available to the appellate court. [18 U.S.C. § 3500(c)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: The statute's objection and preservation procedure must be followed.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: If the United States elects not to obey a § 3500 production order, subsection (d) requires striking the witness's testimony and continuing trial unless the court determines that the interests of justice require a mistrial. [18 U.S.C. § 3500(d)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: Mistrial remains subject to the statutory interests-of-justice determination.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary.

text: As used in § 3500(b), (c), and (d) in relation to a witness called by the United States, “statement” means a written statement made by the witness and signed or otherwise adopted or approved by the witness, a substantially verbatim contemporaneous recording or transcription of the witness's oral statement, or the witness's statement to a grand jury. [18 U.S.C. § 3500(e)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3500)
known_limitations: Notes, summaries, and reports must be tested against the statutory definition rather than labels.
researcher_notes: Official primary sources reviewed; individual, local, circuit, and remedy applications remain within the module's stated boundary. Corrected 2026-10-30 after dual independent source review; draft independently verified; wording owner-approved 2026-10-30.

text: Rule 26.2(a) is reciprocal: after a nondefendant witness testifies on direct, the court must, on motion by a party who did not call the witness, order the calling side to produce a possessed statement relating to the testimony's subject matter. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 26.2(a)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf)

text: Construing the 1974 text of Rule 17(c), *United States v. Nixon* recognized that the subpoena duces tecum was not intended to provide a means of discovery for criminal cases, described the showing lower courts had generally followed (evidentiary and relevant material not otherwise procurable reasonably in advance of trial, need for advance inspection, and good faith rather than a general fishing expedition), and held that the Special Prosecutor must clear three hurdles: relevancy, admissibility, and specificity. *Nixon* expressly did not decide whether a lower standard exists when the subpoena is issued to third parties rather than to government prosecutors. [*United States v. Nixon*, 418 U.S. 683, 698–702 & n.12 (1974)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-418/pdf/USREPORTS-418-683.pdf)

text: Proposed amendments to Rule 17 are pending; they remain proposals, not current Rule 17. After a public-comment period from August 2025 to February 2026, the Standing Committee in June 2026 approved final proposed amendments for submission to the Judicial Conference. text: A *Franks* evidentiary hearing requires a substantial preliminary showing that the affiant included a false statement in the warrant affidavit knowingly and intentionally or with reckless disregard for the truth, and that it was necessary to the finding of probable cause; the attack must be more than conclusory and more than a mere desire to cross-examine, the allegations must be accompanied by an offer of proof, should point out specifically the portion claimed false with supporting reasons, and should be supported by affidavits or sworn or otherwise reliable witness statements or a satisfactory explanation of their absence. Allegations of negligence or innocent mistake are insufficient, and the deliberate falsity or reckless disregard at issue is only that of the affiant, not of any nongovernmental informant. [*Franks v. Delaware*, 438 U.S. 154, 155–56, 171–72 (1978)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-438/pdf/USREPORTS-438-154.pdf)

text: *Miranda* holds that the prosecution may not use statements, whether exculpatory or inculpatory, stemming from custodial interrogation unless it demonstrates the use of procedural safeguards: unless other fully effective means are devised, the specified warnings are required, and a heavy burden rests on the government to demonstrate a knowing and intelligent waiver. Later decisions have reduced the rule's impact while reaffirming its core ruling that unwarned statements may not be used as evidence in the prosecution's case in chief. [*Miranda v. Arizona*, 384 U.S. 436, 444–45, 475, 479 (1966)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-384/pdf/USREPORTS-384-436.pdf); [*Dickerson v. text: Under *Zafiro*, when defendants properly have been joined under Rule 8(b), a district court should grant a severance under Rule 14 only if there is a serious risk that a joint trial would compromise a specific trial right of one of the defendants or prevent the jury from making a reliable judgment about guilt or innocence. text: The Sixth Amendment Speedy Trial Clause protects the accused from arrest or indictment through trial and does not apply once a defendant has been found guilty at trial or has pleaded guilty; *Betterman* reserved whether it applies to bifurcated proceedings in which sentencing-stage facts could increase the prescribed range and whether it reattaches upon renewed prosecution after a successful appeal, and, noting that due process serves as a backstop against exorbitant sentencing delay, expressed no opinion on how Betterman, who advanced no due-process claim, might fare under that standard. text: The Speedy Trial Act and the Sixth Amendment apply different tests: the Act sets day limits, subject to the § 3161(h) exclusions, and a trial-clock violation requires dismissal, with or without prejudice, on the defendant's motion, which is waived if not made before trial or plea; *Barker* found no constitutional basis for quantifying the right into a specified number of days, rejected the demand-waiver rule in favor of balancing length of delay, reason for delay, assertion of the right, and prejudice, and called dismissal the only possible remedy. text: A plea bargain standing alone is without constitutional significance; in itself it is a mere executory agreement which, until embodied in the judgment of a court, does not deprive an accused of liberty or any other constitutionally protected interest. In *Mabry*, the defendant's acceptance of an offer that the prosecutor then withdrew created no constitutional right to specific performance, because his later guilty plea was in no sense induced by the withdrawn offer and his inability to enforce that offer did not impair the voluntariness or intelligence of the plea; as *Mabry* explained, under *Santobello* when a plea rests in any significant degree on a promise or agreement of the prosecutor, so that it can be said to be part of the inducement or consideration, such promise must be fulfilled, although *Santobello* declined to hold that the Constitution compels specific performance of a broken prosecutorial promise as the remedy. [*Mabry v. Johnson*, 467 U.S. 504, 505–10 (1984)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-467/pdf/USREPORTS-467-504.pdf)

text: The remedy for proven lost-offer ineffective assistance must neutralize the taint of the constitutional violation without granting the defendant a windfall. Where resentencing alone will not be full redress, the proper exercise of discretion may be to require the prosecution to reoffer the plea proposal, and in *Lafler* the Court held that the correct remedy was to order the State to reoffer the plea agreement; if the defendant accepts, the trial court has discretion, whose boundaries the Court did not define, to vacate the convictions and resentence under the plea agreement, vacate only some of the convictions and resentence accordingly, or leave the convictions and sentence from trial undisturbed. [*Lafler*, 566 U.S. at 170–71, 174](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-566/pdf/USREPORTS-566-156.pdf)

text: Where counsel's error affected the defendant's understanding of the consequences of pleading guilty, the accepted-plea prejudice inquiry is not defeated categorically by a weak trial defense, though a defendant without any viable defense "will rarely be able to show prejudice from accepting a guilty plea that offers him a better resolution than would be likely after trial"; the inquiry focuses on the defendant's decisionmaking, which may not turn solely on the likelihood of conviction after trial and also involves assessing the respective consequences of a conviction after trial and by plea, and courts should not upset a plea solely because of post hoc assertions but should look to contemporaneous evidence to substantiate the defendant's expressed preferences. text: In a criminal case, before the voir dire examination begins, or within seven days after the defendant discovered or could have discovered, by the exercise of diligence, the grounds therefor, whichever is earlier, the defendant may move to dismiss the indictment or stay the proceedings on the ground of substantial failure to comply with the provisions of title 28 in selecting the grand or petit jury. A motion containing a sworn statement of facts which, if true, would constitute a substantial failure to comply entitles the moving party to present in support of the motion the testimony of the jury commission or clerk, if available, relevant records and papers used by the jury commissioner or clerk that are not public or otherwise available, and any other relevant evidence. Section 1867's procedures are the exclusive means by which a person accused of a federal crime may challenge a jury on the ground that it was not selected in conformity with the provisions of title 28, but they do not preclude any other remedy, civil or criminal, available to vindicate or enforce any law prohibiting discrimination on account of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or economic status in the selection of grand or petit jurors. text: When a jury instruction sets forth all the elements of the charged crime but incorrectly adds one more element, sufficiency is assessed against the elements of the charged crime, not the erroneously heightened instruction, and that limited review does not intrude on the jury's role to resolve conflicts in the testimony and to weigh the evidence. The Court left open several matters: it expressed no view on whether sufficiency must be judged by reference to the elements charged in the indictment when the indictment charges one or more elements not required by statute; it did not suggest that the Government adds an element for sufficiency purposes when the indictment charges different means of committing a crime in the conjunctive; and it did not suggest that an erroneous jury instruction cannot result in reversible error just because the evidence was sufficient to support a conviction. text: If the court enters a judgment of acquittal after a guilty verdict, it must also conditionally determine whether any motion for a new trial should be granted if the judgment of acquittal is later vacated or reversed, and must specify the reasons for that determination; an order conditionally granting a new trial does not affect the finality of the judgment of acquittal. If the court conditionally grants a new trial and an appellate court later reverses the judgment of acquittal, the trial court must proceed with the new trial unless the appellate court orders otherwise. text: The Guidelines direct a sequenced calculation: select the offense guideline, determine the base offense level and specific offense characteristics, apply Chapter Three victim, role, and obstruction adjustments, determine the combined offense level for multiple counts, apply acceptance of responsibility, determine the criminal-history category, determine the guideline range and the Chapter Five sentencing requirements and options, and apply Part K of Chapter Five as appropriate; the court then considers the other applicable § 3553(a) factors. For multiple counts, the amendments effective Nov. 1, 2026 replace the five guidelines in Chapter Three, Part D with a single guideline, § 3D1.1, which determines the combined offense level applicable to all counts; earlier editions grouped the counts under Part D. text: The court uses the Guidelines Manual in effect on the sentencing date unless doing so would violate the ex post facto clause, in which case it uses the Manual in effect on the date the offense of conviction was committed, with the last date of the offense of conviction controlling. The Manual in effect on a particular date is applied in its entirety, but a court applying an earlier edition must consider later amendments to the extent they are clarifying rather than substantive; and if the defendant is convicted of two offenses, the first committed before and the second after a revised edition took effect, the revised edition applies to both. [U.S.S.G. § 1B1.11(a), (b)(1)–(3) & comment. (n.2) (Nov. 1, 2026)](https://www.ussc.gov/guidelines/2026-guidelines-manual/annotated-2026-chapter-1) There is an ex post facto violation when a defendant is sentenced under Guidelines promulgated after the offense and the new version provides a higher applicable Guidelines sentencing range than the version in place at the time of the offense. [*Peugh v. United States*, 569 U.S. 530, 533, 550 (2013)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-569/pdf/USREPORTS-569-530.pdf)

text: Section 3663 provides that the court may order restitution for its covered convictions other than § 3663A(c) offenses, may decline to the extent the complication and prolongation of sentencing outweighs the need for restitution, and may order restitution in any criminal case to the extent agreed in a plea agreement. [18 U.S.C. § 3663A(a)(1), (c)(1)–(2)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3663A?link-type=html) Section 3663A does not apply to its listed property or anti-doping offenses if the court finds, from facts on the record, that the number of identifiable victims makes restitution impracticable or that complex issues of fact would burden sentencing so much that the need for restitution is outweighed. [18 U.S.C. § 3663A(c)(3)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3663A?link-type=html)

text: Unless doing so is impractical, the court must enter a preliminary forfeiture order sufficiently in advance of sentencing to allow the parties to suggest revisions; the order becomes final as to the defendant at sentencing, or at any time before sentencing if the defendant consents, but an order for specific property remains preliminary as to third parties until the ancillary proceeding is concluded. text: Rule 35(b) permits a sentence reduction only on the government's motion: on a motion made within one year of sentencing, if the defendant, after sentencing, provided substantial assistance in investigating or prosecuting another person; on a motion made more than one year after sentencing, only if the defendant's substantial assistance involved one of the information categories in Rule 35(b)(2)(A)–(C). In evaluating substantial assistance the court may consider the defendant's presentence assistance, and when acting under Rule 35(b) the court may reduce the sentence below the statutory minimum. [Fed. R. Crim. P. 35(b)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf) Separately, § 3553(e) gives the court authority, upon motion of the Government, to impose a sentence below a statutory minimum so as to reflect a defendant's substantial assistance in the investigation or prosecution of another person who has committed an offense. text: In a criminal case, a defendant's notice of appeal must be filed in the district court within 14 days after the later of the entry of either the judgment or the order being appealed, or the filing of the government's notice of appeal. Rule 4(b)(3)(A) sets the time to appeal from a judgment of conviction when the defendant timely makes one of the motions it lists. Upon a finding of excusable neglect or good cause, the district court may extend the time to file a notice of appeal for a period not to exceed 30 days from the expiration of the time otherwise prescribed by Rule 4(b). A judgment or order is entered for purposes of Rule 4(b) when it is entered on the criminal docket. [Fed. R. App. P. 4(b)(1)(A)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-appellate-procedure.pdf)

text: Section 3731 provides only for appeals by the United States: from orders dismissing an indictment or information or granting a new trial, except where the Double Jeopardy Clause prohibits further prosecution; from orders suppressing or excluding evidence or requiring the return of seized property, not made after jeopardy attaches and before the verdict, if the United States attorney certifies that the appeal is not taken for delay and the evidence is substantial proof of a material fact; and from orders granting release or denying revocation or modification of release. Each such appeal must be taken within thirty days and diligently prosecuted, and government appeals of sentences are separately governed by § 3742(b). text: Section 3742 separately specifies the defendant's and government's grounds to appeal an otherwise final sentence and the appellate court's disposition authority; a disagreement with sentence alone is not a substitute for a statutory ground. The government may not further prosecute a sentence appeal without the personal approval of the Attorney General, the Solicitor General, or a designated deputy solicitor general. Under a plea agreement that includes a specific sentence, a defendant may not appeal under § 3742(a)(3) or (4) unless the sentence imposed is greater than the agreed sentence. text: Within 14 days after filing the notice of appeal or entry of an order disposing of the last timely remaining motion of a type specified in Rule 4(a)(4)(A), whichever is later, an appellant must either order the needed transcript parts in writing (stating any Criminal Justice Act payment and filing a copy of the order with the district clerk within the same period) or file a certificate that no transcript will be ordered. Satisfactory payment arrangements must be made with the reporter at the time of ordering. Unless the entire transcript is ordered, the appellant must, within the same 14 days, file a statement of the issues the appellant intends to present and serve on the appellee a copy of the order or certificate and the statement; an appellant who will argue that a finding or conclusion is unsupported by or contrary to the evidence must include in the record a transcript of all evidence relevant to that finding or conclusion. text: Under Rule 31(a)(1), the appellant must serve and file a brief within 40 days after the record is filed, and the appellee must serve and file a brief within 30 days after the appellant's brief is served. The appellant may serve and file a reply brief within 21 days after service of the appellee's brief, but a reply brief must be filed at least 7 days before argument, unless the court, for good cause, allows a later filing. Under Rule 31(a)(2), a court of appeals that routinely considers cases on the merits promptly after the briefs are filed may shorten the time to serve and file briefs, either by local rule or by order in a particular case. text: A petition for rehearing en banc must begin with a statement that the panel decision conflicts with a decision of the court to which the petition is addressed (with citation to the conflicting case or cases) and the full court's consideration is therefore necessary to secure or maintain uniformity of the court's decisions; that the panel decision conflicts with a decision of the United States Supreme Court (with citation to the conflicting case or cases); that the panel decision conflicts with an authoritative decision of another United States court of appeals (with citation to the conflicting case or cases); or that the proceeding involves one or more questions of exceptional importance, each concisely stated. Rehearing en banc is not favored and ordinarily will be allowed only if one of those criteria is met. [Fed. R. text: Under Rule 3(d), a motion filed by an inmate confined in an institution is timely if deposited in the institution's internal mailing system on or before the last day for filing; if the institution has a system designed for legal mail, the inmate must use it to receive the benefit of the rule. text: Section 2255(f) supplies a one-year limitation period that runs from the latest of four separately worded dates: the date on which the judgment of conviction becomes final, or one of three other dates that apply only on their own terms: the date on which an impediment to making a motion created by governmental action in violation of the Constitution or laws of the United States is removed, if the movant was prevented from making a motion by that action; the date on which the right asserted was initially recognized by the Supreme Court, if that right has been newly recognized by the Supreme Court and made retroactively applicable to cases on collateral review; or the date on which the facts supporting the claim could have been discovered through the exercise of due diligence. [28 U.S.C. § 2255(f)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/28/2255)

text: In the circumstances presented there, an evident miscalculation of the elapsed time, *Day* held that district courts are permitted, but not obliged, to consider sua sponte the timeliness of a state prisoner's habeas petition, under a limitation defense that is not jurisdictional, even though the State did not correctly raise it. Before acting on its own initiative, the court must accord the parties fair notice and an opportunity to present their positions, must assure itself that the petitioner is not significantly prejudiced by the delayed focus on the limitation issue, and must determine whether the interests of justice would be better served by addressing the merits or by dismissing the petition as time barred; it would be an abuse of discretion to override a State's deliberate waiver of a limitations defense. *Day* addressed a state prisoner's petition under § 2244(d)'s one-year limitation. text: Section 2255 reaches sentences imposed in violation of the Constitution or laws of the United States, sentences imposed without jurisdiction, sentences in excess of the maximum authorized by law, and sentences otherwise subject to collateral attack. [28 U.S.C. § 2255(a)–(b)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/28/2255) The remedy does not encompass all claimed errors: outside jurisdictional and constitutional claims, an error of law does not provide a basis for collateral attack unless it constituted "a fundamental defect which inherently results in a complete miscarriage of justice." [*United States v. Addonizio*, 442 U.S. 178, 185 (1979)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-442/pdf/USREPORTS-442-178.pdf); [*Hill v. United States*, 368 U.S. 424, 428 (1962)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-368/pdf/USREPORTS-368-424.pdf)

text: A nonconstitutional violation of a criminal rule is not automatically cognizable: in *Hill*, the failure to invite the defendant to speak before sentence was neither jurisdictional nor constitutional, was not a fundamental defect inherently resulting in a complete miscarriage of justice or an omission inconsistent with the rudimentary demands of fair procedure, and did not present exceptional circumstances where the need for the remedy is apparent. The Court decided only that § 2255 relief is unavailable when all that is shown is a failure to comply with the formal requirements of Rule 32(a), leaving open violations occurring with other aggravating circumstances. [*Hill v. United States*, 368 U.S. 424, 428–29 (1962)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-368/pdf/USREPORTS-368-424.pdf)

text: A sentencing judge's disappointed expectation about later Parole Commission administration of a lawful sentence was not a § 2255 defect in *Addonizio*: the judge has no enforceable expectations about actual release, and later Commission actions, whether or not they accord with the judge's expectations at sentencing, do not retroactively affect the validity of the final judgment. Absent a claim of constitutional error or lack of jurisdiction, or a sentence outside statutory limits, collateral relief requires an error of fact or law of the "fundamental" character that renders the entire proceeding irregular and invalid. [*United States v. Addonizio*, 442 U.S. 178, 185–90 (1979)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-442/pdf/USREPORTS-442-178.pdf)

text: Strickland deficiency asks whether counsel's acts or omissions fell below an objective standard of reasonableness under prevailing professional norms, judged on the facts of the particular case as of the time of counsel's conduct. The defendant must identify the challenged acts or omissions, and judicial scrutiny is highly deferential: a court must indulge a strong presumption that counsel's conduct falls within the wide range of reasonable professional assistance, which the defendant must overcome. [*Strickland v. Washington*, 466 U.S. 668, 688–90 (1984)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-466/pdf/USREPORTS-466-668.pdf)

text: *Lee* applied *Hill v. Lockhart*'s test, a reasonable probability that but for counsel's errors the defendant would not have pleaded guilty and would have insisted on going to trial. It rejected a per se rule that a defendant with no viable defense cannot show prejudice, because categorical rules are ill suited to an inquiry that demands a case-by-case examination, and directed courts not to upset a plea solely because of post hoc assertions but to look to contemporaneous evidence to substantiate a defendant's expressed preferences. In the unusual circumstances of that case, where deportation was the determinative issue, the Court found a reasonable probability, backed by substantial and uncontroverted evidence, that Lee would have rejected the plea; answering the Government's argument under *Padilla*, it could not say rejecting the plea would have been irrational. [*Lee v. United States*, 582 U.S. 357, 366–71 (2017)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-582/pdf/USREPORTS-582-357.pdf)

text: Counsel performs deficiently by disregarding a defendant's specific instructions to file a notice of appeal, while a defendant who explicitly tells counsel not to file an appeal cannot later complain that counsel followed that instruction. Where the defendant has not clearly conveyed his wishes one way or the other, *Flores-Ortega* imposes a duty to consult about an appeal when there is reason to think either that a rational defendant would want to appeal or that this particular defendant reasonably demonstrated to counsel an interest in appealing, and prejudice requires a reasonable probability that, but for the deficient failure to consult, the defendant would have timely appealed. [*Roe v. Flores-Ortega*, 528 U.S. 470, 477–84 (2000)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-528/pdf/USREPORTS-528-470.pdf)

text: For an error in the sentencing calculation itself, *Glover* rejected a minimum-increase requirement for Strickland prejudice: authority does not suggest that a minimal amount of additional time in prison cannot constitute prejudice, and the Court's jurisprudence suggests that any amount of actual jail time has Sixth Amendment significance. Under a determinate system of constrained discretion such as the Sentencing Guidelines, the size of the increase cannot bar a prejudice showing, though it may be a factor in assessing deficient performance, which still must be proven. [*Glover v. United States*, 531 U.S. 198, 203–04 (2001)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-531/pdf/USREPORTS-531-198.pdf)

text: Section 2255(h) requires that a second or successive § 2255 motion be "certified as provided in section 2244 by a panel of the appropriate court of appeals" to contain one of the two showings listed in § 2255(h). *Bowe v. United States* explained that this cross-reference incorporates § 2244(b)(3)(A)–(D), which require a motion in the appropriate court of appeals for an order authorizing the district court to consider the filing, determination of that motion by a three-judge panel, a prima facie showing, and a grant or denial "not later than 30 days after the filing of the motion." *Bowe* observed in a parenthetical, without deciding the point, that "most Courts of Appeals view that requirement as advisory." Section 2244(b)(3)(E) provides that the grant or denial of an authorization "shall not be appealable and shall not be the subject of a petition for rehearing or for a writ of certiorari." *Bowe* held that § 2255(h)'s cross-reference does not clearly incorporate § 2244(b)(3)(E)'s certiorari bar, so a federal prisoner is not prohibited from seeking certiorari from a panel's denial of authorization to file a second or successive § 2255 motion. *Bowe* did not decide whether § 2244(b)(3)(E)'s panel-rehearing bar applies to federal prisoners, so rehearing practice must be checked under current controlling circuit law. The statutes do not prescribe the motion's form, attachments, length limits, filing method, or service; those matters require the current rules and forms of the particular court of appeals. [28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(3)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/28/2244); [28 U.S.C. § 2255(h)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/28/2255); [*Bowe v. United States*, 607 U.S. 13, 18, 28–36 (2026)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/607us1r04_n7ip.pdf)

text: AO 242 is the federal judiciary's national petition form for § 2241 and asks for the conviction or detention information, grounds, facts, administrative-remedy history, requested relief, and a declaration under penalty of perjury. Its instructions say the petitioner must send copies of the decisions being challenged and of any briefs or administrative remedy forms filed, must include the $5 filing fee required by 28 U.S.C. § 1914(a) or ask to proceed in forma pauperis, and should mail the petition to the clerk for the district and division of confinement; the form names the warden or other authorized person having custody as respondent, and § 2242 requires a signed and verified application naming the custodian, if known. Local rules may also apply, for example page limits on a separate legal memorandum, and an in forma pauperis request must include the documents the court requires, so check the filing district's current local rules. text: Under *Padilla*, a § 2241 petitioner who challenges present physical custody within the United States, including domestic military detention, should name the warden as respondent and file the petition in the district of confinement. Those defaults do not answer a challenge to a form of custody other than present physical confinement, such as a detainer for confinement to be imposed in the future under *Braden*; *Padilla* also noted a long, implicitly recognized exception in the military context for an American citizen detained outside the territorial jurisdiction of any district court, who may name a supervisory official as respondent and file in the district where that respondent resides, and declined to resolve whether the Attorney General is a proper respondent for an alien detained pending deportation. Identify the custody being challenged before choosing the respondent and district. text: Under Jones v. Hendrix, the saving clause in § 2255(e) preserves recourse to § 2241 for challenges to detention other than collateral attacks on a sentence. For example, a prisoner might wish to argue that he is being detained in a place or manner not authorized by the sentence, that he has unlawfully been denied parole or good-time credits, or that an administrative sanction affecting the conditions of his detention is illegal. Section 2255 is the ordinary vehicle for a collateral attack on a federal sentence, and Congress generally barred federal prisoners authorized to apply for relief by § 2255 motion from applying for a writ of habeas corpus under § 2241. AEDPA's restrictions on § 2255 are best understood as restrictions on § 2255, not as expansions of § 2241's applicability. [*Jones v. Hendrix*, 599 U.S. 465, 473–78 (2023)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/22pdf/599us1r42_2b35.pdf); [28 U.S.C. § 2241(c)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/28/2241)

text: Under *Jones*, the saving clause ensures that § 2255(e) does not displace § 2241 when a prisoner challenges the legality of his detention without attacking the validity of his sentence, for example by arguing that he is detained in a place or manner not authorized by the sentence, has unlawfully been denied parole or good-time credits, or faces an illegal administrative sanction affecting the conditions of his detention. AO 242 likewise treats a claim that the Bureau of Prisons miscalculated a sentence or failed to properly award good time credits as a challenge to the way a sentence is being carried out. Section 2241(c) provides that the writ does not extend to a prisoner unless one of its listed conditions applies; § 2241(c)(3) covers a prisoner in custody in violation of the Constitution or laws or treaties of the United States. text: COA classification and the permissible custody remedy are addressed separately in the § 2241 appeal-and-relief module. text: Rule 21 requires a petition titled “In re [name of petitioner],” filed with the circuit clerk, served on all parties, and copied to the trial-court judge; it must state the relief sought, the issues presented, the necessary facts, and the reasons the writ should issue, and include any order or opinion or essential parts of the record. The clerk dockets the petition upon receiving the docket fee; the court may deny it without an answer but otherwise must order the respondent, if any, to answer within a fixed time. Unless the court permits otherwise, the petition may not exceed 7,800 words if computer-produced or 30 pages if handwritten or typewritten (excluding the required attachments), and an original and 3 copies must be filed unless a local rule or order requires a different number. [Fed. R. App. P. 21(a)–(b), (d)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-appellate-procedure.pdf)

text: DOJ's current guidance states that a full presidential pardon removes penalties and disabilities, including a firearm disability, resulting from the federal conviction, but that a person who also has a separate, independent basis for firearm prohibition, like a state conviction or a prohibiting status, may need to seek federal firearms relief. The Attorney General may also restore federal firearms rights under 18 U.S.C. § 925(c); DOJ states that relief under that process removes only applicable federal firearms disabilities and does not override independent restrictions imposed by state law. text: Rule 35(a)'s correction authority is narrow. The 1991 committee note, written when the provision was Rule 35(c) (the 2002 note says former Rule 35(c) "is now located in Rule 35(a)"), says the authority "is intended to be very narrow and to extend only to those cases in which an obvious error or mistake has occurred in the sentence." It "is not intended to afford the court the opportunity to reconsider the application or interpretation of the sentencing guidelines or for the court simply to change its mind about the appropriateness of the sentence," and it should not "be used to reopen issues previously resolved at the sentencing hearing through the exercise of the court’s discretion with regard to the application of the sentencing guidelines." text: Within 14 days after sentencing, the court may correct a sentence that resulted from arithmetical, technical, or other clear error, and Rule 35(c) defines "sentencing" as "the oral announcement of the sentence," so the 14 days run from the oral announcement. The advisory committee's note to the 1991 amendment, written when this authority was Rule 35(c), says it "is intended to be very narrow and to extend only to those cases in which an obvious error or mistake has occurred in the sentence," and contemplates that the order correcting the sentence "must be entered within" the period then allowed. text: *Wade v. United States* held in the § 3553(e) and Guideline § 5K1.1 context that district courts may review a government refusal to file a substantial-assistance motion and grant a remedy if the refusal was based on an unconstitutional motive; accepting the government's concession, the Court also said relief would be available if the refusal "was not rationally related to any legitimate Government end." A showing of assistance is necessary but not sufficient, since the government may refuse based on "its rational assessment of the cost and benefit," and generalized allegations of improper motive do not entitle a defendant to a remedy, discovery, or a hearing. [*Wade v. United States*, 504 U.S. 181, 185–87 (1992)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-504/pdf/USREPORTS-504-181.pdf)

text: An alleged government promise to make or consider a Rule 35(b) motion presents a distinct agreement question: under *Santobello*, a prosecutor's promise must be fulfilled when a plea rests in any significant degree on it, "so that it can be said to be part of the inducement or consideration," and *Puckett* treats plea bargains as "essentially contracts," applies plain-error review to a forfeited breach claim, and recognizes rescission or specific performance as possible remedies. Neither case involved a Rule 35(b) motion or a post-sentencing cooperation promise, so applying them to such a promise extends their holdings. That question is not resolved merely by labeling the cooperation substantial. [*Santobello v. New York*, 404 U.S. 257, 262–63 (1971)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-404/pdf/USREPORTS-404-257.pdf); [*Puckett v. text: Although Rule 36 says "at any time," a pending appeal can affect district-court authority; for a timely motion the court lacks authority to grant because of an appeal that has been docketed and is pending, Rule 37(a) lets the court defer, deny, or state that it would grant the motion if the court of appeals remands or that the motion raises a substantial issue. If the court so states, Rule 37(b) requires the movant to promptly notify the circuit clerk under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 12.1, and under Rule 37(c) the court may decide the motion if the court of appeals remands for that purpose; Rule 37 does not define when an appeal limits district-court authority, which is subject to controlling circuit law. text: In a criminal case, the defendant's notice is due within 14 days, and the government's within 30 days, after the later of entry of the judgment or order appealed or the filing of the other side's notice of appeal, and, for an appeal from a judgment of conviction, a timely motion listed in Rule 4(b)(3)(A) resets the defendant's period. An inmate's notice is timely under Rule 4(c)(1) if it is deposited in the institution's internal mail system (its legal-mail system, if it has one) on or before the last day for filing and either is accompanied by the required declaration, notarized statement, or evidence (such as a postmark or date stamp) showing deposit and prepaid postage, or the court of appeals permits the later filing of a declaration or notarized statement; when a defendant files under Rule 4(c), the government's 30 days run from the later of entry of the judgment or order appealed or the district court's docketing of the defendant's notice under Rule 4(c)(3); and under Rule 4(b)(4), the district court may extend the time by no more than 30 days from the expiration of the original period upon a finding of excusable neglect or good cause. [Fed. R. App. P. 4(b)–(c)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-appellate-procedure.pdf)

text: Under PS 5160.06, the Bureau designates a state institution for concurrent service of a federal sentence when the federal sentencing court ordered, recommended, or expressed an intention of concurrency, or when it finds the designation appropriate after reviewing the five § 3621(b) factors. On an inmate's nunc pro tunc request, the Bureau must consider the request but has no obligation to grant it; it seeks the sentencing court's position and decides under the five § 3621(b) factors, deciding without the court's view if no response is received after at least 60 days. No letter to the court is needed if the court previously ordered, recommended, or made clear its intention for consecutive service, and the Bureau will not allow a concurrent designation if the sentencing court has already determined the order of service. A separate procedure applies to inmates sentenced in the Fourth Circuit between Dec. 29, 2006 and Mar. 27, 2012 (*Mangum II*). [BOP PS 5160.06 §§ 1.a, 5.d, 6](https://www.bop.gov/policy/progstat/5160_006.pdf); [18 U.S.C. § 3621(b)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3621)
