text: In *Spencer*, release after filing did not defeat the § 2254 "in custody" requirement, but once the sentence has expired "some concrete and continuing injury" (some "collateral consequence") must exist for the case to continue, and the party seeking jurisdiction bears the burden "clearly to allege facts" showing it. The Court declined to presume collateral consequences from a parole revocation, and the capable-of-repetition exception "applies only in exceptional situations" where the challenged action is too short to be fully litigated and the same party reasonably expects to face it again. [*Spencer v. Kemna*, 523 U.S. 1, 7–18 (1998)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-523/pdf/USREPORTS-523-1.pdf)

text: Under § 3585, prior-custody credit turns on when the sentence commenced, what official detention preceded that date and on what charge, and whether that time was credited against another sentence. The Bureau's Sentence Computations page states that information such as arrests or periods of prior custody is not public information and may not be released by telephone or internet, and that its release "can only be obtained by submitting a written request with an original authorization form that has been signed by the inmate"; an inmate housed at a Bureau institution should raise computation questions with Correctional Systems staff and, if not satisfied, may appeal through the Administrative Remedy process. text: A sentence computation involves distinct statutory steps: the concurrent or consecutive relationship of the terms (§ 3584(a)), treatment of multiple terms as a single aggregate term for administrative purposes (§ 3584(c)), commencement (§ 3585(a)), and prior-custody credit (§ 3585(b)), with good-conduct time credited separately (§ 3624(b)). For offenses committed on or after November 1, 1987, the Bureau's initial projected release date assumes the maximum possible good-conduct time and "is subject to change during the inmate's incarceration." [18 U.S.C. § 3584(a), (c)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3584); [18 U.S.C. § 3585(a)–(b)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3585); [18 U.S.C. § 3624(b)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3624); [28 C.F.R. § 523.20(b)(1)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title28-vol2/pdf/CFR-2025-title28-vol2-sec523-30.pdf)

text: A sentencing-court recommendation is one of the matters the Bureau considers in designating a place of imprisonment, a court order or recommendation for community-corrections placement has "no binding effect" on the Bureau's placement authority, and a designation "is not reviewable by any court." text: Immigration status has no single consequence shared by every case: a prisoner is ineligible to apply FSA time credits if subject to a final order of removal, while an immigration detainer is a request that the custodial agency advise DHS before the alien's release. For designation, BOP policy awards no points for ICE detainers but reviews each case to determine whether the Deportable Alien public safety factor applies; that factor covers an inmate who is not a U.S. citizen, is not applied (or is removed) when ICE or the Executive Office for Immigration Review has determined that deportation proceedings are unwarranted or there is a finding not to deport, is not applied if the inmate has been naturalized, and when applied requires housing in at least a Low security level institution. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees are not eligible for RDAP early release. [18 U.S.C. § 3632(d)(4)(E)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3632); [8 C.F.R. § 287.7(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-8/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-287/section-287.7); [BOP PS 5100.08 CN-3, ch. 4, p. 12; ch. 5, p. 9](https://www.bop.gov/policy/progstat/5100_008_cn-3.pdf); [28 C.F.R. § 550.55(b)(1)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-28/chapter-V/subchapter-C/part-550/subpart-F)

text: Article III permits a prisoner serving a term of imprisonment, against whom a detainer has been lodged on an untried charge pending in another party State, to request final disposition; trial must occur within 180 days after the prisoner has caused written notice and the request, accompanied by the custodian's certificate and forwarded through the warden by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, to be delivered to the prosecuting officer and the appropriate court. The court may grant a necessary or reasonable continuance only for good cause shown in open court, the prisoner or counsel being present, and the period is tolled whenever and for as long as the prisoner is unable to stand trial. text: Article IV entitles the prosecutor who has lodged a detainer to obtain temporary custody on a written request, provided the court having jurisdiction has duly approved, recorded, and transmitted the request and a 30-day period has passed in which the Governor of the sending State (for the United States, the Attorney General) may disapprove it on his own motion or the prisoner's. text: The UDC will ordinarily review an incident report within five work days after it is issued, not counting the day it was issued, weekends, and holidays (review may be suspended during a criminal-prosecution investigation), and may find that the prisoner committed the act, find that the prisoner did not, or refer the report to the DHO. The UDC will automatically refer a Greatest or High severity charge, or the report of an inmate covered by § 541.4, to the DHO. text: When prison discipline threatens an already-created good-time interest, *Wolff v. McDonnell* requires advance written notice of the charges, with no less than 24 hours to prepare; an opportunity to call witnesses and present documentary evidence when doing so will not be unduly hazardous to institutional safety or correctional goals; and a written statement of the evidence relied on and reasons, but does not constitutionalize the full criminal-trial process. An illiterate inmate, or one facing an issue too complex to present alone, should be free to seek a fellow inmate's aid or, if that is forbidden, adequate substitute aid from staff or a sufficiently competent inmate designated by staff. text: Under the First Step Act regulation, a prisoner may lose earned FSA Time Credits for violating the requirements or rules of an evidence-based recidivism reduction program or productive activity, through the part 541 discipline procedures, whose sanctions table also lists forfeiture of earned FSA Time Credits as a sanction for prohibited acts; by statute, any loss requires written notice and is limited to credits earned as of the date of the rule violation. text: First Step Act home confinement requires 24-hour electronic monitoring (or, if electronic monitoring is infeasible for technical or religious reasons, alternative means that the Director determines are as effective or more effective), requires the prisoner to remain in the residence except to leave, subject to the Director's approval, for the purposes the statute lists: a job or job-related activities or job-seeking, assigned recidivism-reduction programming or productive activities (or similar activities), community service, crime victim restoration activities, medical treatment, religious activities, and family-related activities that facilitate reentry, and, except as provided in § 3624(g)(4), requires the prisoner to remain in home confinement until serving not less than 85 percent of the imposed term. The Director may modify the § 3624(g)(2)(A)(i) monitoring, residence, and other conditions if the Director determines that a compelling reason exists and that the prisoner has demonstrated exemplary compliance, and shall, to the extent practicable, provide that increasingly less restrictive conditions be imposed on prisoners who demonstrate continued compliance. For a violation, the Director may impose additional conditions or revoke prerelease custody, and shall revoke it for a nontechnical violation. [18 U.S.C. § 3624(g)(2)(A), (g)(4), (g)(5)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3624)

text: The current First Step Act time-credit regulation, as amended effective September 30, 2026, provides that the Bureau may apply FSA Time Credits toward prerelease custody or early transfer to supervised release under § 3624(g) only if the inmate meets the § 523.44(b) criteria (credits equal to the remainder of the imposed term, demonstrated risk reduction or maintained minimum or low risk on periodic reassessments, and a computed remainder of the term). Prerelease custody also requires the § 523.44(c) criteria: minimum or low risk through the last two risk and needs assessments, or a warden-approved petition. Early transfer to supervised release requires the (c) criteria plus the § 523.44(d) criteria: minimum or low risk through the last assessment, a supervised-release term imposed by the sentencing court, and transfer no earlier than 12 months before it would otherwise have occurred. The Bureau may not apply credits for an inmate subject to a final order of removal. It also generally may not apply credits to a term imposed for an offense under laws other than the U.S. Code, but § 523.44(a)(3) recognizes exceptions for a D.C. Code sentence when application is authorized by the D.C. Code and for a sentence imposed in a foreign country for which the U.S. Parole Commission has determined an equivalent U.S. Code sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 4106A. Lost credits may be restored in part or in full, case by case, after clear conduct for two consecutive risk and needs assessments. [28 C.F.R. §§ 523.43(c), 523.44](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-28/chapter-V/subchapter-B/part-523/subpart-E); [91 Fed. Reg. 55,740, 55,743–44 (Aug. 31, 2026) (interim final rule)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-31/pdf/2026-17752.pdf)

text: A May 28, 2025 BOP press release describes a directive from the Director instructing staff to expand the use of home confinement for eligible individuals under the First Step Act and Second Chance Act. It says the policy is meant to ensure that eligible individuals, particularly those who do not require transitional services at Residential Reentry Centers (RRCs), are transferred to home confinement as soon as statutorily possible. Home confinement is a priority for eligible individuals who do not require the structured support of an RRC, and RRC placement will be reserved for those with the greatest need. The release also says that decisions will be based on each person's needs, support systems and readiness for reintegration; that Unit Teams must use FSA and SCA Conditional Placement Dates to guide prerelease planning; and that staff must distinguish between FSA and SCA eligibility criteria and understand the limits of each statute, particularly when determining the duration of prerelease custody, while there is no restriction on how many FSA time credits may be applied toward home confinement. [BOP, Expanding Home Confinement (press release, May 28, 2025)](https://www.bop.gov/news/pdfs/20250528-home-confinement-expansioin.pdf)

text: When a § 2241 habeas petitioner challenges his present physical custody within the United States, the default rule is that the proper respondent is the warden of the facility where the prisoner is being held, and he should file the petition in the district of confinement. District courts are limited to granting habeas relief within their respective jurisdictions, which requires nothing more than that the court issuing the writ have jurisdiction over the custodian. [28 U.S.C. § 2241](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/28/2241); [*Rumsfeld v. Padilla*, 542 U.S. 426, 434–47 (2004)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-542/pdf/USREPORTS-542-426.pdf)

text: Sections 3624(c) and (g) assign prerelease-custody and early-transfer functions to the Bureau of Prisons Director. text: Section 3624(a) directs the Bureau to release a prisoner on the date the term of imprisonment expires, less any time credited under § 3624(b). Section 3624(d) requires the Bureau, on release at the expiration of the term, to furnish the prisoner with: (1) suitable clothing; (2) an amount of money, not more than $500, that the Director determines is consistent with the offender's needs and the public interest, unless the Director determines that the offender's financial position is such that no sum should be furnished; and (3) transportation to the place of conviction, to the prisoner's bona fide residence within the United States, or to another place within the United States that the Director authorizes. [18 U.S.C. § 3624(a), (d)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3624)

text: After *Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo*, courts must exercise independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority, "as the APA requires," rather than defer to an agency interpretation simply because a statute is ambiguous, while respecting a statute's delegation of authority to an agency consistent with constitutional limits and ensuring the agency acts within it; the holdings of prior Chevron-based cases that specific agency actions are lawful remain subject to statutory stare decisis. text: Section 2241(a) authorizes the district courts to grant the writ "within their respective jurisdictions," and § 2241(c) requires a listed ground, such as custody under federal authority or in violation of federal law; for core habeas petitions challenging present physical confinement, the immediate custodian is the proper respondent and jurisdiction lies in only one district, the district of confinement. Throughout the case the petitioner "must have suffered, or be threatened with, an actual injury traceable to the defendant and likely to be redressed by a favorable judicial decision," and § 3625 makes 5 U.S.C. §§ 554, 555, and 701–706 inapplicable to determinations under its subchapter. BOP policy notes that "[i]n many cases, courts require a proper Appeal to the General Counsel before an inmate may pursue the complaint in court." text: For a grievance alleging sexual abuse, the agency may not impose a time limit on submission or require informal resolution, and must ensure the prisoner can submit it without submitting it to, and that it is not referred to, a staff member who is the subject of the complaint; otherwise-applicable time limits may still apply to any portion that does not allege sexual abuse. text: The term starts on "the day the person is released from imprisonment" and does not run during any period in which the person is imprisoned in connection with a conviction for a Federal, State, or local crime unless the imprisonment is for less than 30 consecutive days. text: Before modifying the conditions of probation or supervised release, Rule 32.1(c)(1) requires the court to hold a hearing, at which the person has the right to counsel and an opportunity to make a statement and present any information in mitigation. Under Rule 32.1(c)(2), a hearing is not required if: (A) the person waives the hearing; or (B) the relief sought is favorable to the person and does not extend the term of probation or of supervised release; and (C) an attorney for the government has received notice of the relief sought, has had a reasonable opportunity to object, and has not done so. Section 3006A(a)(1)(E) requires each district's plan to provide representation for any financially eligible person who faces modification, reduction, or enlargement of a condition of supervised release. text: Beyond the conditions § 3583(d) makes mandatory, the court may order as a further condition any discretionary probation condition in § 3563(b) or any other condition it considers appropriate, such as treatment, search, monitoring, residence, travel, association, contact, employment, financial, and disclosure conditions, but only "to the extent that such condition" is reasonably related to the listed § 3553(a) factors, involves no greater deprivation of liberty than is reasonably necessary, and is consistent with pertinent Sentencing Commission policy statements. Section 3583(d) separately states that the court "shall order" certain conditions, including no new crime, no unlawful possession of a controlled substance, and refraining from unlawful use of a controlled substance with drug testing; that drug-use-and-testing condition may be ameliorated or suspended as provided in § 3563(a)(4). Section 3583(d) also separately authorizes, in their own sentences, a condition that an alien defendant subject to deportation be deported and remain outside the United States, and a search condition for a person who is a felon and required to register under the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act. text: Under Rule 32.1(c)(1), before modifying the conditions of probation or supervised release, the court must hold a hearing, at which the person has the right to counsel and an opportunity to make a statement and present any information in mitigation. Under Rule 32.1(c)(2), a hearing is not required if "(A) the person waives the hearing; or (B) the relief sought is favorable to the person and does not extend the term of probation or of supervised release; and (C) an attorney for the government has received notice of the relief sought, has had a reasonable opportunity to object, and has not done so." Section 3583(e)(2) provides that the court may, after considering the factors set forth in § 3553(a)(1), (a)(2)(B), (a)(2)(C), (a)(2)(D), (a)(4), (a)(5), (a)(6), and (a)(7), "modify, reduce, or enlarge the conditions of supervised release, at any time prior to the expiration or termination of the term of supervised release, pursuant to the provisions of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure relating to the modification of probation and the provisions applicable to the initial setting of the terms and conditions of post-release supervision". [Fed. R. Crim. P. 32.1(c) (Dec. 1, 2025 ed.)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-criminal-procedure.pdf); [18 U.S.C. § 3583(e)(2)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3583)

text: The Fourth Circuit recognizes administrative exhaustion as a judicial restraint that can make a § 2241 petition premature, but not as a jurisdictional prerequisite to the district court's habeas power. [*Dragenice v. Ridge*, 389 F.3d 92, 98 (4th Cir. 2004)](https://www.ca4.uscourts.gov/opinions/036717.P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fourth Circuit. Dragenice involved immigration detention and a pending removal proceeding, not the BOP Part 542 remedy program, so it does not establish BOP-specific steps or exceptions.

text: In the Fifth Circuit, a federal prisoner challenging a Parole Commission decision ordinarily must exhaust before § 2241 review; an exception requires extraordinary circumstances such as an unavailable or wholly inappropriate remedy or a patently futile course, and the prisoner bears the burden. [*Fuller v. Rich*, 11 F.3d 61, 62 (5th Cir. 1994)](https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/Opinions/pub/93/93-01767.CR0.wpd.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fifth Circuit and limited to a Parole Commission administrative appeal. The opinion required presentation even when the appeal might be rejected as untimely and does not excuse BOP Part 542 exhaustion on speculation alone.

text: In the Sixth Circuit, federal prisoners ordinarily must exhaust before filing under § 2241, but the judge-made requirement may be excused where remedies are futile or cannot provide the relief sought, or where the administrator—not the prisoner—caused the failure; a missing final response does not automatically defeat exhaustion. [*Fazzini v. Northeast Ohio Correctional Center*, 473 F.3d 229, 231–36 (6th Cir. 2006)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/796434/paul-fazzini-v-northeast-ohio-correctional-center-warden-united-states/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Sixth Circuit and arising from a Parole Commission appeal. The opinion's treatment of what must be attached at pleading is distinct from whether a particular BOP Part 542 claim was properly exhausted.

text: The Seventh Circuit applies a common-law exhaustion rule to § 2241 even though the PLRA's statutory exhaustion rule does not apply; judge-made exceptions exist, but the hurdle is high and self-created delay does not establish an excuse. [*Richmond v. Scibana*, 387 F.3d 602, 604–06 (7th Cir. 2004)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/788163/michael-richmond-v-joseph-scibana-warden-federal-correctional/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Seventh Circuit. Richmond ultimately classified the placement-policy challenge outside § 2241, so the common-law exhaustion proposition must not be converted into a merits holding that every BOP placement challenge sounds in habeas.

text: In the Eighth Circuit, a prisoner challenging the BOP's execution of a federal sentence must first present the claim to the BOP; failure to request the available BOP designation required dismissal of the § 2241 petition without prejudice. [*Mathena v. United States*, 577 F.3d 943, 946 (8th Cir. 2009)](https://ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov/opndir/09/08/082184P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eighth Circuit and limited to the available nunc pro tunc designation process in the sentence-execution posture. No general exception rule is inferred.

text: In the Tenth Circuit, exhaustion of available BOP remedies is a prerequisite to § 2241 relief despite the absence of an express statutory clause; a narrow futility exception exists, but alleged local categorical denial is insufficient where regional and national review remain available. [*Garza v. Davis*, 596 F.3d 1198, 1203–04 (10th Cir. 2010)](https://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/sites/ca10/files/opinions/01018368252.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Tenth Circuit and limited to the BOP placement posture. A prisoner cannot establish futility merely by styling the claim as a facial regulatory challenge, but materially different facts require separate analysis.

text: In the First Circuit, appellate review of a First Step Act § 404 ruling is deferential absent a legal benchmark error; the district court may explain its exercise of discretion briefly, and the explanation may be understood from the full record, but it must show consideration of the parties' nonfrivolous arguments. [*United States v. Rodríguez-Reyes*, No. 23-2037, slip op. at 9–15 (1st Cir. June 10, 2026)](https://www.ca1.uscourts.gov/sites/ca1/files/opnfiles/23-2037P-01A.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the First Circuit. Rodríguez-Reyes does not require a detailed rebuttal to every argument or a sentence reduction, and the adequacy of an explanation remains record dependent.

text: In the Second Circuit, a district court is not categorically required to hold a hearing at which the defendant is present before denying a First Step Act § 404 sentence-reduction motion. [*United States v. Gadsden*, 982 F.3d 106, 112–15 (2d Cir. 2020)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-ca2-19-03139/pdf/USCOURTS-ca2-19-03139-0.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Second Circuit and limited to the absence of a categorical hearing-and-presence requirement before denial. Gadsden does not prohibit a hearing, resolve every due-process question, or excuse compliance with Concepcion's later nationwide explanation rule.

text: In the Third Circuit, a First Step Act § 404 movant ordinarily is not entitled to a plenary resentencing hearing at which he would be present, and neither the original sentencing judge nor a reassigned judge is required to hold an in-person hearing; the court must still articulate a brief statement of reasons demonstrating that it considered the parties’ arguments. Where the movant requested a hearing or, alternatively, leave to file a sentencing memorandum, the district court erred by denying him “either a hearing or a reasonable opportunity to present his sentencing arguments in writing.” The court of appeals commended, but declined to mandate, a specific multistep procedure that several district courts in the circuit had adopted, which includes giving the parties an opportunity to file sentencing memoranda. [*United States v. Shields*, 48 F.4th 183, slip op. at 14–20 (3d Cir. 2022)](https://www2.ca3.uscourts.gov/opinarch/192717p.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Third Circuit. Shields does not create an entitlement to oral allocution or a plenary resentencing; its error finding turned on denying both a hearing and the requested opportunity for written sentencing submissions in the circumstances presented.

text: In the Fourth Circuit, § 404 does not require a reduction even when the existing sentence exceeds a revised statutory maximum, but the record must demonstrate that the district court considered every nonfrivolous argument presented; an ambiguous record can require vacatur and remand. [*United States v. Reed*, 58 F.4th 816, 819–23 (4th Cir. 2023)](https://www.ca4.uscourts.gov/opinions/197368.P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fourth Circuit. Reed recognizes that Concepcion displaced Collington's mandatory-reduction rule; it does not guarantee a reduction or make every sparse order reversible.

text: In the Fifth Circuit, § 404(c)'s bar on a later motion after a prior merits denial is a mandatory claim-processing rule rather than a jurisdictional limit; when the government properly invokes the bar and the first motion received a complete merits review, the court must enforce it. [*United States v. Naranjo*, 102 F.4th 280, 283–85 (5th Cir. 2024)](https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/22/22-50938-CV0.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fifth Circuit and limited to § 404(c)'s successive-motion bar. Naranjo does not resolve hearing rights, the merits of an initial motion, or whether a materially different prior disposition was a complete merits review.

text: In the Sixth Circuit, the § 404 benchmark recalculation incorporates only the Fair Sentencing Act's retroactive changes; the court then may consider other relevant intervening information, must reason through nonfrivolous arguments, and must explain the decision adequately for abuse-of-discretion review. [*United States v. Domenech*, 63 F.4th 1078, 1083–86 (6th Cir. 2023)](https://www.opn.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/23a0059p-06.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Sixth Circuit. Domenech does not require the benchmark Guidelines range to absorb nonretroactive changes and does not require a reduction; reassignment on remand was tied to the repeated failures in that record.

text: In the Seventh Circuit, the adequacy of a § 404 explanation is context dependent; a district court abuses its discretion when a materially changed record presents new nonfrivolous arguments and the ruling effectively repeats an earlier order without showing that those arguments were considered. [*United States v. Williams*, 93 F.4th 389, 391–94 (7th Cir. 2024)](https://media.ca7.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/OpinionsWeb/processWebInputExternal.pl?Path=Y2024%2FD02-20%2FC%3A23-2313%3AJ%3AWood%3Aaut%3AT%3AfnOp%3AN%3A3170766%3AS%3A0&Submit=Display)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Seventh Circuit. Williams does not prescribe a required explanation length or guarantee relief; it addresses a current record materially different from the one underlying the earlier order.

text: In the Eighth Circuit, eligibility under § 404 is reviewed de novo and the grant or denial of an eligible motion is reviewed for abuse of discretion; the First Step Act does not require a hearing on the motion. [*United States v. McDonald*, 944 F.3d 769, 771–72 (8th Cir. 2019)](https://ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov/opndir/19/12/191221P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eighth Circuit. McDonald's no-hearing and review holdings survive as bounded propositions; any pre-Concepcion restriction on intervening information is not adopted.

text: In the Ninth Circuit after Concepcion, a district court deciding a § 404 motion must consider the parties' nonfrivolous arguments based on intervening legal or factual developments and give a brief statement of reasons; an unexplained denial can require vacatur and remand. [*United States v. Carter*, 44 F.4th 1227, 1228–29 (9th Cir. 2022)](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/08/17/19-10411.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Ninth Circuit. Carter recognizes that Concepcion abrogated Kelley's contrary intervening-change restriction; it does not require a reduction or a detailed point-by-point opinion.

text: In the Tenth Circuit, a § 404 proceeding is a sentence modification rather than a plenary resentencing; no hearing or defendant presence is categorically required, and the discretionary disposition is reviewed for abuse of discretion with enough reasoning to permit review. [*United States v. Mannie*, 971 F.3d 1145, 1155–58 (10th Cir. 2020)](https://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/sites/ca10/files/opinions/010110393562.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Tenth Circuit. Mannie's surviving nonplenary, hearing, presence, and review holdings are used; any pre-Concepcion restriction on intervening information is not adopted.

text: In the Eleventh Circuit, denial of an eligible § 404 motion is reviewed for abuse of discretion; a court may deny relief even when the existing sentence exceeds the revised statutory maximum, may not use § 404 as a collateral vehicle to invalidate the original sentence, and may satisfy Concepcion with a brief explanation evident from the record. [*United States v. Williams*, 63 F.4th 908, 912–14 (11th Cir. 2023)](https://media.ca11.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/files/202112877.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eleventh Circuit. Williams does not permit a court to ignore nonfrivolous arguments, require a reduction, or decide an independent collateral attack through § 404.

text: In the D.C. Circuit, § 404 does not create a categorical right to allocution before decision; after Concepcion, review of the discretionary ruling is not overly searching absent legal error, a sentence above the revised maximum does not itself compel reduction, and a sufficiently reasoned record can sustain denial. text: In the First Circuit, the certificate-of-appealability and appellate preclearance requirements do not directly apply to a federal prisoner's claim that actually proceeds under § 2241; whether a filing is properly classified under § 2241 rather than § 2255 remains a separate question. known_limitations: Binding only in the First Circuit and limited to the COA consequence after correct classification. Barrett involved alternative § 2255, § 2241, and All Writs Act theories; no saving-clause merits rule is adopted, and current filing-office instructions should be checked before filing.

known_limitations: Binding only in the Fifth Circuit and limited to the COA rule after correct § 2241 classification. Jeffers's saving-clause merits analysis is not adopted and must be read in light of later Supreme Court law.

text: In the Eighth Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s filing prerequisite is a mandatory claim-processing rule that must be enforced when properly raised; an unexhausted motion is dismissed without prejudice, and asserted futility based on the Attorney General's home-confinement memorandum did not excuse the missing request. text: In the Ninth Circuit, § 3582(c)(1)(A)'s defendant-filing prerequisite is a mandatory claim-processing rule enforced when the government invokes it; a renewed motion based on changed circumstances required a new qualifying BOP request, and the filing defect was not cured by the passage of 30 days while the motion was pending. known_limitations: Binding only in the Ninth Circuit and limited to a later motion premised on changed circumstances. Keller does not establish a universal issue-exhaustion test for every supplemental fact or argument.

text: In the First Circuit, a pending appeal from a supervised-release revocation does not divest the district court of its continuing § 3583(e)(2) authority to modify release conditions during the term of supervision. [*United States v. D'Amario*, 412 F.3d 253, 255–56 (1st Cir. 2005)](https://www.ca1.uscourts.gov/sites/ca1/files/opnfiles/04-2566-01A.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the First Circuit and limited to continuing modification jurisdiction while a revocation appeal was pending. D'Amario does not establish an early-termination standard, a changed-circumstances rule, or a universal hearing rule.

text: In the Second Circuit, a court deciding whether to modify or terminate supervised release must consider the § 3583(e) subset of § 3553(a) factors, but it need not make a separate factual finding on each factor; a statement, read with the record, that the statutory factors were considered is sufficient. [*United States v. Gammarano*, 321 F.3d 311, 315–16 (2d Cir. 2003)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/781046/united-states-v-john-gammarano/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Second Circuit. Gammarano does not require a particular explanation length, create a presumption of termination, or decide whether changed circumstances are required for condition modification; Parisi separately clarifies that they are not.

text: In the Third Circuit, a district court need not find an exceptional, extraordinary, new, or unforeseen circumstance before granting early termination under § 3583(e)(1), although Melvin states that early termination generally will be proper only when the judge is satisfied that new or unforeseen circumstances warrant it. [*United States v. Melvin*, 978 F.3d 49, slip op. at 6–7 (3d Cir. 2020)](https://www2.ca3.uscourts.gov/opinarch/201158p.pdf) The court may terminate supervision only after the expiration of one year of supervised release and only if satisfied that termination is warranted by the defendant’s conduct and the interest of justice. [18 U.S.C. § 3583(e)(1)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3583)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Third Circuit. Melvin disavows a threshold prerequisite but does not guarantee relief for compliance, eliminate factor consideration, or prescribe the result on remand.

text: In the Fourth Circuit, § 3583(e)(1), in the typical case, allows a conduct-based inquiry into the continued necessity for supervision after the individual has served one full year on supervised release, and its interest-of-justice language permits consideration of a broad range of factors; the court must conclude that termination is warranted both by the individual’s conduct and by the interest of justice. The statute is not a mechanism for collaterally attacking an original, unappealed sentence. [*United States v. Pregent*, 190 F.3d 279, slip op. at 6–7 (4th Cir. 1999)](https://www.ca4.uscourts.gov/opinions/Published/986309.P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fourth Circuit. Pregent reviewed denial for abuse of discretion and did not create entitlement to termination whenever conduct and interests of justice favor relief; the original-sentence challenge belongs in the procedurally proper review vehicle.

text: In the Fifth Circuit, changed circumstances are not a jurisdictional prerequisite to modifying a supervised-release condition under § 3583(e)(2), but illegality alone is not one of the enumerated grounds and cannot itself supply the basis for modification. [*United States v. Caillier*, 79 F.4th 506, 509–12 (5th Cir. 2023)](https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/22/22-30383-CR0.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fifth Circuit. Caillier permits modification for statutory reasons such as deterrence and public safety even when an invalid original condition prompted review; it does not allow § 3583(e)(2) to replace direct or collateral review of legality.

text: In the Sixth Circuit, § 3583(e)(1) does not make exceptionally good behavior an absolute prerequisite to early termination, though such behavior remains a relevant consideration, and the court said it “might expect” district courts to “generally” find early termination proper only when exceptionally good conduct or other changed circumstances are present. [*United States v. Hale*, No. 24-5362, slip op. at 3–5 (6th Cir. Jan. 30, 2025)](https://www.opn.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/25a0022p-06.pdf) A district court may terminate supervision only after the expiration of one year of supervised release, only after considering the listed § 3553(a) factors, and only if satisfied that termination is warranted by the defendant’s conduct and the interest of justice. [18 U.S.C. § 3583(e)(1)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/3583)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Sixth Circuit. Hale rejects a categorical threshold and vacated for use of the wrong standard; it does not hold ordinary compliance sufficient or direct that termination be granted.

text: In the Seventh Circuit, an early-termination ruling must give some indication that the district court considered the statutory factors; a blanket policy of waiting until only twelve months of supervision remain circumvents § 3583(e)(1)'s individualized process. [*United States v. Lowe*, 632 F.3d 996, 998–99 (7th Cir. 2011)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-ca7-10-02832/pdf/USCOURTS-ca7-10-02832-0.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Seventh Circuit. Lowe does not require findings on every factor or a hearing on every motion; it requires a reviewable indication of factor consideration and rejects the categorical timing policy used there.

text: In the Eighth Circuit, Rule 32.1(c)(1) applies only when a court modifies conditions, so the rule does not require a hearing or counsel before a court denies a motion to terminate supervision or modify conditions. Applying Mosby, Norris held that a district court that had presided over the case since its inception was not required to explain its denial of early termination of supervised release, and acknowledged that the Eighth Circuit “is routinely cited as the outlier” on this point. [*United States v. Norris*, 62 F.4th 441, slip op. at 8, 13–15 & n.4 (8th Cir. 2023)](https://ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov/opndir/23/03/213849P.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eighth Circuit and limited to denial. Rule 32.1 ordinarily requires a hearing and counsel before an actual condition modification unless an enumerated exception applies; Norris does not authorize an unexplained denial when the record supplies no discernible basis.

text: In the Ninth Circuit, § 3583(e)(1) does not impose a threshold requirement of exceptional or extraordinary circumstances, exceptionally good behavior, or undue hardship before a court may consider early termination. text: In the Tenth Circuit, § 3583(e)(2) does not require changed circumstances before a district court may modify supervised-release conditions; the court must instead consider the listed factors, follow Rule 32.1, and ensure the new conditions satisfy the requirements applicable to supervised-release conditions. [*United States v. Begay*, 631 F.3d 1168, 1171–73 (10th Cir. 2011)](https://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/sites/ca10/files/opinions/01018581211.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Tenth Circuit. Begay addresses condition modification, not early termination, and does not dispense with factor consideration, Rule 32.1 procedure, or substantive limits on the modified condition.

text: In the First Circuit, assuming audita querela survives in federal criminal cases, it can address only a legal objection arising after conviction that is not redressable through another postconviction remedy; equitable hardship alone is insufficient. [*United States v. Holder*, 936 F.2d 1, 2–5 (1st Cir. 1991)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/563216/united-states-v-ewart-mark-holder/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the First Circuit. Holder expressly did not decide whether audita querela survives; it rejected a pure-equity immigration-consequence theory and did not identify any actual remedial gap. Section 2255 classification and the current nationwide limits, including Jones v. Hendrix, still must be applied independently.

text: In the Second Circuit, audita querela "remains available in limited circumstances with respect to criminal convictions": it "is probably available" for a legal objection that arose after the conviction and is not redressable through another post-conviction remedy, and it would lie if the absence of any avenue of collateral attack would raise serious constitutional questions. Because *Booker* is not retroactive on collateral review, Richter presented no colorable constitutional claim, so the absence of other avenues raised no serious constitutional questions and the writ did not lie. [*United States v. Richter*, 510 F.3d 103, 104 (2d Cir. 2007)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1389954/united-states-v-richter/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Second Circuit. Richter did not hold that the writ lies in any actual case, did not make statutory nonretroactivity a constitutional defect, and predates Jones v. Hendrix; no post-Jones expansion or exception is inferred.

text: In the Third Circuit, the All Writs Act is residual and cannot displace § 2255: a federal-sentence claim cognizable under § 2255 cannot be recast as audita querela, and prior use of § 2255 or the successive-motion gate does not create a gap. [*Massey v. United States*, 581 F.3d 172, 174 (3d Cir. 2009) (per curiam)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1266166/massey-v-united-states/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Third Circuit. Massey involved a Booker sentencing claim by a prisoner who had already pursued § 2255; it does not establish that audita querela survives or define relief outside § 2255's field.

text: In the Fifth Circuit, assuming audita querela survives in criminal cases, it is limited to a postjudgment legal objection unavailable through another postconviction remedy; purely equitable grounds are insufficient. [*United States v. Miller*, 599 F.3d 484, 488–90 (5th Cir. 2010)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/71483/united-states-v-miller/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Fifth Circuit. Miller left survival of the writ open and arose from a restitution-offset request; its actual disposition does not establish that AEDPA limits, nonretroactivity, or hardship alone creates a gap.

text: In the Seventh Circuit, audita querela would require a legal defense or discharge arising after judgment; equity, harsh collateral consequences, or gross injustice alone does not satisfy that requirement. [*United States v. Johnson*, 962 F.2d 579, 581–83 (7th Cir. 1992)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/582608/united-states-v-manapurath-eappen-johnson/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Seventh Circuit. Johnson declined to decide the writ's ultimate survival and addressed a deportation consequence after conviction; no broader gap or § 2255-circumvention rule is inferred beyond the opinion's express limits.

text: In the Tenth Circuit, *Torres*, assuming without deciding that audita querela survives, held as one of two alternative grounds that the writ is "not available to a petitioner when other remedies exist, such as a motion to vacate sentence under 28 U.S.C. § 2255." As the other ground, it held that a prisoner who had already filed a § 2255 motion could not avoid the successive-motion bar "by simply styling a petition under a different name," so the filing was properly treated as a successive § 2255 motion requiring authorization. *Torres* distinguished circuit precedent limiting recharacterization of a filing that would be a first § 2255 motion; that question is now governed by *Castro*, under which a court cannot recharacterize a pro se filing as a first § 2255 motion unless it informs the litigant of its intent, warns that later § 2255 motions will be subject to the second-or-successive restrictions, and provides an opportunity to withdraw or amend the filing. [*United States v. Torres*, 282 F.3d 1241, 1245–46 & n.6 (10th Cir. 2002)](https://storage.courtlistener.com/pdf/2002/02/21/United_States_vs._Torres.pdf); [*Castro v. United States*, 540 U.S. 375, 377, 383 (2003)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-540/pdf/USREPORTS-540-375.pdf); [28 U.S.C. § 2255(h)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/28/2255)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Tenth Circuit. Torres assumed without deciding that audita querela might survive, distinguished coram nobis by custody, and tied notice before recharacterization to whether the filing would be the prisoner's first § 2255 motion.

text: In the Eleventh Circuit, audita querela may not be granted when the challenge is cognizable under § 2255; after recharacterization, an unauthorized second or successive motion remains outside the district court's jurisdiction. [*United States v. Holt*, 417 F.3d 1172, 1174–75 (11th Cir. 2005) (per curiam)](https://media.ca11.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/files/200415848.pdf)
known_limitations: Binding only in the Eleventh Circuit. Holt did not hold that audita querela survives for claims outside § 2255; it addressed a constitutional sentencing attack by a prisoner with a prior § 2255 motion and an absent successive-motion authorization.

text: In the D.C. Circuit, a federal court can vacate a conviction through audita querela "only if the writ permits a defendant to raise a legal objection not cognizable under existing federal postconviction remedies," and *Ayala* did not decide whether the writ ever supplies that basis; it called the authority to use a "pure equity" variant "open to serious doubt" without resolving the point, because the appellant had abandoned his equitable claims. A claim cognizable under § 2255 belongs there. [*United States v. Ayala*, 894 F.2d 425, 429–30 (D.C. Cir. 1990)](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/535569/united-states-v-wilfredo-felix-ayala/)
known_limitations: Binding only in the D.C. Circuit. Ayala did not definitively decide whether the writ survives, rejected an immigration-consequence equity theory, and remanded for treatment under § 2255 without deciding the constitutional merits.
